23 March 2026 ATP 4-02.11 ix Preface Army Techniques Publication (ATP) 4-02.11 serves as a primary doctrine reference for holistic casualty response. Implementation of the techniques presented in this publication enable Service members to execute casualty response, render first aid, and prevent greater harm to injured Service members. The principal audience for ATP 4-02.11 is Army personnel as well as employees of civilian agencies executing and supporting operations. Commanders, staffs, and subordinates ensure their decisions and actions comply with applicable United States, international, and in some cases host-nation laws and regulations. Commanders at all levels ensure that their Service members operate in accordance with the law of armed conflict and the rules of engagement. Refer to Field Manual 6-27/Marine Corps Tactical Publication 11-10C for more information on The Commander’s Handbook on the Law of Land Warfare. This publication implements or is in consonance with the following North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) Standardization Agreement (STANAG) and the standards of the American, British, Canadian, Australian, and New Zealand (ABCANZ) standards: TITLE NATO STANAG ABCANZ Aeromedical Evacuation 3204 CBRN First Aid Handbook 2358 Coalition Health Interoperability Handbook 256 First Aid Dressings, First Aid Kits, and Emergency Medical Care Kits 2126 Land Operational Reports 2020 NATO Land Urgent Voice Messages (LUVM) Pocket Book 2627 Pre-Hospital Combat Casualty Care Standards for ABCANZ Soldiers 2121 Requirement for Training in Casualty Care for All Military Personnel 2122 Tactical Combat Casualty Care Card 2136 ATP 4-02.11 uses joint terms where applicable. Selected joint and Army terms and definitions appear in both the glossary and the text. Terms for which ATP 4-02.11 is the proponent publication (the authority) are bold and italicized in the text and are marked with an asterisk (*) in the glossary. For other term definitions shown in the text, the term is italicized, and the number of the proponent publication follows the definition. This publication applies to the Active Army, Army National Guard/Army National Guard of the United States, and United States Army Reserve unless otherwise stated. Throughout this publication, as appropriate, reference is made to the major policy guidance affecting each specific topic. These references should not be considered as the only policy guidance available. When issues arise that require consideration of policy guidance, the issue should be thoroughly researched and, as appropriate, coordinated with the supporting staff judge advocate, governmental or nongovernmental agency involved. The Army proponent and preparing agency of ATP 4-02.11 is the United States Army Medical Center of Excellence. 23 March 2026 ATP 4-02.11 xi Introduction ATP 4-02.11 provides discussion on casualty response and first aid procedures for nonmedical personnel in environments from home station to combat situations. This publication is meant to be used by trainers and individuals being trained based on common first aid tasks. These tasks are meant to reinforce and maintain proficiency in the correct procedures for providing first aid throughout a Service member’s time in Service. ATP 4-02.11 is designed to facilitate training and first aid competencies by bridging first aid training across the spectrum of assignments from initial military training to permanent duty station and deployment. ATP 4- 02.11 introduces Tactical Combat Casualty Care (TCCC) with first aid tasks and procedures associated with combat situations. Training scenarios can be completed by combining individual and multiple first aid tasks with collective tasks. 23 March 2026 ATP 4-02.11 1 289BPART ONE 292BCASUALTY RESPONSE Casualty response is of paramount importance to military units and leaders in winning our Nations’s wars and providing a critical role in ensuring the welfare and effectiveness of the armed forces. In the unpredictable and high-stakes environment of warfare, casualties are an unfortunate reality. Whether it is injuries sustained on the battlefield or the loss of fellow Service members, casualty response encompasses the immediate and long-term actions taken to mitigate the impact of these incidents. Effective casualty response saves lives but also boosts the morale of troops, enhances unit cohesion, allows leaders to maintain operational readiness, and win our Nations’s wars. Chapter 1 Casualty Response 195BCASUALTY RESPONSE OVERVIEW 1-1. Casualty response is the immediate and organized care, evacuation and reporting of those injured or killed in action. Casualty response is a leader driven system designed to synchronize the planning, rehearsal, and execution of individual and collective tasks required to complete the mission while improving casualty outcomes. Due to the nature of military operations both at home and in combat, nonmedical Service members must sometimes rely on themselves and other Service members to render first aid until medical assistance arrives. Self-aid, buddy aid, and combat lifesaver (CLS) support is normally the first care a casualty receives in an operational setting and is provided until medically trained personnel (combat medic, corpsman, or medical technician) arrive to begin treatment. 1-2. First responder care includes self-aid, buddy aid, CLS tasks, and Tactical Combat Casualty Care (TCCC). Care provided by first responders is not limited to Service members but is provided to all those requiring initial treatment, stabilization, and when necessary, movement to higher roles of care for further treatment. 1-3. First responder care varies by Service, with the core training focused on TCCC. The application of TCCC occurs anywhere in the pre-hospital setting and can be tailored by the Joint Trauma System (JTS) to support Service-specific mission requirements. The TCCC training has four individual tiers or sets of responsibilities (see table 1-1 on page 2): • Self-aid or buddy aid. • Combat lifesaver. • Combat medic or corpsman. • Combat paramedic and provider. 1-4. Department of Defense Instruction (DODI) 1322.24, directs standardized combat casualty care training for all Service members and Department of Defense (DOD)-expeditionary civilians. According to DODI 1322.24, all Service members will be trained and proficient in basic lifesaving TCCC skills. The TCCC skills replace legacy military first aid skills. This evidence-based approach to combat casualty care reflects the lessons of nearly two decades of war and has the potential to reduce preventable prehospital trauma-related deaths.

Casualty Response 23 March 2026 ATP 4-02.11 3 1-5. The JTS established the standard of care for TCCC or prehospital medicine in the operational environment for the DOD. The JTS is part of the Defense Health Agency (also known as DHA) providing clinical practice guidelines (CPG)s and performance improvement for all levels of military trauma care. The Committee on Tactical Combat Casualty Care (CoTCCC) also supports the JTS. The committee is composed of representatives from the Army and Air Force and are responsible for developing CPGs for the delivery of TCCC in the operational environment. 196BTERMINOLOGY 1-6. A thorough understanding of the fundamentals of casualty response can save a life, prevent permanent disability, or reduce long periods of hospitalization. Knowledge of key terms used in Army and joint doctrine helps Service members better understand and appreciate the role they play in providing first aid in tactical and nontactical environments. Knowledge of the fundamentals of casualty response and key terminology also helps Service members understand when and how to provide first aid in all settings. 1-7. A casualty is any person who is lost to the organization by having been declared dead, duty status – whereabouts unknown, excused absence-whereabouts unknown, missing, ill, or injured. (Joint Publication [JP] 4-02). The casualty classification is given to a Service member prior to treatment by medical personnel. A Service member who is wounded and conducts self-aid or is given treatment by a CLS is still classified as a casualty. That Service member is then moved to a casualty collection point (CCP) where medical personnel conduct triage and treatment of that casualty. Once treated by medical personnel, the Service member is now classified as a patient and enters the roles of medical care. Once a casualty is deceased, they become human remains and should be separated from the patient flow. The requirements for handling human remains are different and specifically explained in ATP 4-46. Service specific procedures should be followed when providing aid, evacuation, and reporting of combat casualties. 1-8. A casualty collection point is a location that may or may not be staffed, where casualties are assembled for evacuation to a medical treatment facility with medical personnel (ATP 4-02.2). The CCPs are normally predesignated along the axis of advance or evacuation routes. Forward of the Role 1 battalion aid station (BAS), the combat medic or corpsman, CLS, and Service members take casualties to the CCPs. A battalion aid station is the forward-most medically staffed treatment location organic to the maneuver battalion (ATP 4-02.4). These points facilitate acquisition of casualties by supporting ambulance teams and reducing evacuation time. When used by the BAS, CCPs help preserve BAS mobility, preclude carrying casualties forward, and reduce evacuation time to the sustainment area. 1-9. Casualty evacuation is the unregulated movement of casualties aboard any vehicle. Also called CASEVAC (JP 4-02). The Army defines casualty evacuation as the movement of casualties aboard nonmedical vehicles or aircraft without en route medical care (ATP 4-02.13). If a casualty is moved to a medical treatment facility (MTF) in a nonmedical vehicle without en route care provided by a medically trained Service member (such as a combat medic or corpsman) then the TCCC should be continually performed while the casualty is being transported. Casualties transported in this manner do not normally receive en route medical care. If the casualty is acquired by a dedicated medical vehicle with a medically trained crew, the role of first aid ceases, and the casualty becomes the responsibility of the Military Health System chain and is then referred to as a patient. 1-10. The core principles of casualty response include self-aid or buddy aid (first responder care), medical treatment (provided by combat medics, corpsmen, or medical technicians), and leader responsibilities (such as security, scene control, establishing a CCP, monitoring personnel, managing casualty movement, fulfilling reporting requirements, and coordinating evacuation). These principles must be thoroughly rehearsed and executed to maximize survivability in any operational environment. While these principles remain constant, the specific conditions in which they are applied can vary widely and are relevant to both military operations and civilian incident responses. This adaptability ensures that the response strategies are effective in different settings and enhances the overall efficacy of emergency management. 1-11. Joint Publication 4-02 defines combat lifesaver as a Nonmedical Department of Defense person who has received additional trauma training and equipment, providing enhanced medical treatment beyond self- aid or buddy aid. (JP 4-02). The United States (U.S.) Army defines a combat lifesaver as a Soldier trained and equipped to provide enhanced first aid as a secondary mission, known as CLS. Enhanced first aid is the measures which require an additional level of training above self-aid and buddy aid. The CLS provides

Chapter 1 4 ATP 4-02.11 23 March 2026 this level of enhanced first aid and treats the most common causes of death on the battlefield, which are massive hemorrhage, airway and/or respiratory problems. The CLS also taught the skills to prevent complications and treat others associated but not life-threatening injuries. A minimum of one individual per squad, crew, team, or equivalent-sized unit should be trained. The primary duty of this individual does not change. The additional duty of a CLS is to provide enhanced first aid for injuries based on their training before the combat medic or corpsman arrives. 1-12. First aid is the immediate lifesaving measures performed on casualties or military working animals. Every Service member is trained to be proficient in a variety of specific first aid procedures on injured personnel. This training enables the Service member or a buddy to apply immediate first aid measures to alleviate a life-threatening situation on an injured person. Select Soldiers are trained to perform first aid on military working animals. For additional information on first aid for military working animals refer to the deployed medicine website. 1-13. A first responder is anyone who provides initial and immediate treatment to self or others. (JP 4-02) First responders play a crucial role in casualty response by providing immediate aid, including hemorrhage control and airway management, and improving the chances of survival for wounded personnel in the operational environment. 1-14. Medical evacuation is the timely and effective movement of the wounded, injured, or ill to and between medical treatment facilities on dedicated and properly marked medical platforms with en route care provided by medical personnel. Also called MEDEVAC (ATP 4-02.2). 1-15. A medical treatment facility is a facility established for the purpose of furnishing medical and/or dental care to eligible individuals. Also called MTF (JP 4-02). The Army defines a medical treatment facility as any facility established for the purpose of providing medical treatment (FM 4-02). This includes battalion aid stations, Role 2 facilities, dispensaries, clinics, and hospitals. 1-16. Medical treatment is the care and management of wounded, injured, or ill Service members by medically trained, certified or credentialed personnel. It may include emergency medical treatment (EMT), advanced trauma management, and resuscitative and surgical intervention. 1-17. Joint services define a patient as a sick, injured, wounded, or other person receiving medical care, dental care, or other medical treatment (JP 4-02). The U.S. Army defines a patient as a wounded, ill and injured Soldier who receives medical care or treatment from medically trained personnel (ATP 4-02.10). Once the casualty has entered the medical continuum of care (combat medic, corpsman, evacuation crew, or MTF), the role of first aid in the care of the casualty ceases and the casualty becomes the responsibility of the Military Health System. Once the casualty has entered the Military Health System they are referred to as a patient. 1-18. Tactical Combat Casualty Care is the deliberate integration of tactics and medicine to treat casualties during combat. Also called TCCC (JP 4-02). The unit standard operating procedure (SOP) and operation order should address TCCC procedures and casualty evacuation (CASEVAC) in detail to include aid for chemical casualties with particular emphasis on lifesaving tasks. The SOP should cover the duties and responsibilities of essential personnel, the evacuation of chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) contaminated casualties (on routes separate from non-contaminated casualties), and priority for operating essential weapons and positions. The SOP should specify preferred and alternate methods of evacuation, and the SOP should make provisions for retrieving and safeguarding the weapons, ammunition, and equipment of casualties. Slightly wounded personnel are treated at the appropriate role of care and returned to duty as soon as possible. CASEVAC and medical evacuation (MEDEVAC) should be rehearsed like other critical parts of an operation. 1-19. Triage is the system of sorting and prioritizing casualties based on the tactical situation, mission, and available resources (FM 4-02). Casualties are sorted and categorized in one of the treatment categories (immediate [I], delayed [D], minimal [M], and expectant [E]) prior to being taken to the treatment areas. This sorting occurs at the triage point and is called the "IDME" or the "DIME." See paragraph 3-87 on page 38 for additional information on the triaging of casualties.

Casualty Response 23 March 2026 ATP 4-02.11 5 197BCASUALTY COLLECTION POINT OPERATIONS 1-20. When designating a CCP, the unit commander determines if medical personnel will be at the CCP. This decision is based upon the assessment of risk versus the availability of personnel. Medical personnel may not be available to staff these points, and CLS and ambulatory patients may be required to perform self-aid, buddy aid, or CLS support. The CCPs should be identified on watercraft, operational overlays, and planned by phase for operations. The CCP planning considerations include site security, proximity to the landing zone (LZ), cover and concealment, and access to evacuation routes. Leaders should provide guidance on aid and litter teams, distribution of casualty equipment, and proper avoidance of choke points. Medical personnel are responsible for activity inside the CCP, and the supported unit leaders are responsible for activity outside the CCP. 1-21. It is essential for units to meticulously plan the movement of casualties from the point of injury (POI) to supporting Role 3 MTF. Medical staff and unit leaders must be well-versed in the flow of casualties, extending their understanding at least two levels above their own. This encompasses knowledge of medical regulating, casualty tracking, and hospitalization protocols. For instance, platoon leaders and their medics should clearly know the path a casualty takes once they depart from the company CCP and BAS. Similarly, company leaders and senior medics should be familiar with the trajectory of a casualty beyond the BAS and through the Role 2 MTF. 1-22. Moreover, it is vital to consider potential changes in the designated Role 3 MTF, which may occur when crossing a phase line or when the capacity of a facility is reached. Medical personnel must stay informed about these variables and regularly update themselves on their current status. This will ensure that the casualty care and evacuation chain remain efficient and responsive to dynamic operational conditions. 1-23. Leaders must be able to answer the following questions to establish the tactical casualty flow: • Where are the casualties being evacuated to? • Will ground, air, or water assets conduct evacuation to the CCP? • How will evacuation be conducted to the CCP? • What are the distances and times of travel? • Will expected casualties be able to make it that far? If not, what parts of the plan need to be corrected? • Who will evacuate the casualties (CASEVAC or MEDEVAC)? • Are medical assets positioned to ensure continuity of care? 25BSITE SELECTION 1-24. The CCP layout (see figure 1-1 on page 6) site is addressed during the planning phase of the military decision-making process, or troop leading procedures (commonly known as TLPs). Tactical battle plans will vary depending on the type and number of units incorporated in the plan. Mission variables are always a factor for CCP site selection during operations.

Chapter 1 6 ATP 4-02.11 23 March 2026 Figure 1-1. Casualty collection point layout in an open area or field 1-25. The location of the CCP will depend on the unit location, the tactical situation, and the number of casualties to be evacuated. The unit first sergeant determines the location of the company CCP, or the platoon sergeant for the platoon CCP with guidance from the respective combat medics. Battle drills and the tactical SOP should be established on how casualties will be moved from the POI to the CCP. 1-26. The company CCP should be in a covered and concealed position in the company trains area while the platoon CCP should be located at the platoon’s rear. The CCP should be: • Away from natural or enemy choke points. • Covered and concealed. • Expandable if casualty load increases. • In a building or on a hardstand (exclusive CCP building limits confusion). • In an area with good drainage. • Inside the perimeter and allow for passive security. • Near lines of patient drift, or natural routes along which wounded Soldiers may be expected to go back for medical care from a combat position. • Near and have access to evacuation routes (foot, vehicle, and aircraft). • Near templated areas of expected high casualties. • Next to objective choke points. • Reasonably close to the fight. • Trafficable to evacuation assets. Note. “Lines of Drift” are paths of least resistance that offer the greatest ease while considering obstacles and modes of transit to the objective. 1-27. Establishing a CCP in a building (see figure 1-2 on page 7) may be the only choice when conducting operations in urban areas. After the unit ensures that the building is cleared and secured, leaders— • Determine the structural, environmental, medical, and CBRN hazards prior to receiving casualties. • Determine location of control point and triage. • Minimize congestion. • Remove or relocate furniture or obstructions.

Casualty Response 23 March 2026 ATP 4-02.11 7 • Consider rigid litter or non-rigid pole-less litter for movement. • Use largest rooms possible. • Separate treatment categories by room. If triage categories are separated by walls, it is more difficult to monitor all the casualties. • Color-code and mark rooms by treatment categories. Figure 1-2. Casualty collection point in a building 26BCASUALTY COLLECTION POINT SITE SELECTION 1-28. The CCP site selection is addressed during troop leading procedures and the CCP SOP should be rehearsed. The CCP should be established with: • A day and night marking system. • A triage point for entry into and exit from the CCP to track casualties and control access. • Properly marked evacuation categories for day and night (non-tactical or tactical) operations. • A killed in action (KIA) area away from the other casualties. • A medical resupply area. • A helicopter landing zone (commonly known as HLZ). 1-29. The first sergeant or platoon sergeant is responsible for casualty flow and everything outside the CCP. They— • Provide for CCP structure and organization (color coded per tactical SOP for both day and night). • Maintain command and control and situational awareness. • Control aid and litter teams. • Ensure security is established and maintained. • Remove, collect, identify, organize, and maintain casualty equipment outside of the treatment area. • Track casualties and equipment into and out of CCP. • Establish accountability and send reports to higher. • Move casualties through CCP entrance and exit control point. 1-30. Medical personnel are responsible for operations inside the CCP. Medical personnel assigned to the CCP include the: • Triage officer or noncommissioned officer who sorts and organizes the casualties into appropriate treatment categories.

Chapter 1 8 ATP 4-02.11 23 March 2026 • Medics, corpsman, or medical technicians who organize medical equipment and supplies. • Medical personnel, CLS, and aid and litter teams who assist with treatment and packaging of casualties. 1-31. Once triaged, casualties categorized as "Minimal" should ideally stay with their assigned unit or assist with security at the CCP, if possible. Deceased personnel are designated as KIA. Their remains should stay with the assigned unit until mortuary affairs personnel arrive, or until the remains are transferred to a morgue. The mortuary affairs SOP should clearly outline the handling of the remains, considering theater-specific requirements, environmental factors, and the religious beliefs of the Service member. 1-32. It is also important to note that the remains of deceased personnel should not be moved with patients on MEDEVAC ambulances. This practice helps maintain the dignity of the deceased and ensures the focus remains on providing urgent care to the living casualties during MEDEVAC. 198BCASUALTY RESPONSE FOR UNITED STATES ARMY UNITS 1-33. The treatment and evacuation of casualties are difficult tasks for an organization to execute due to the operating distance away from its higher headquarters. Units should allocate adequate assets to the platoon to assist in casualty treatment and evacuation. Platoon medics evaluate and treat sick and injured Soldiers and assist the unit in the evacuation of casualties. 27BCASUALTY CARE 1-34. When casualties occur, the platoon must provide aid to those wounded in action. Combat medics, who are assisted by nonmedical personnel, provide EMT to alleviate potentially life-threatening injuries and to ensure maximum survivability. This support is commonly provided by enlisted personnel and includes first aid (self-aid or buddy aid), enhanced first aid by the CLS, and EMT by the platoon medic. 295BWounded in action 1-35. The ability of fellow Soldiers to provide aid to wounded comrades is heavily influenced by the tactical situation. Minimizing casualties is more achievable when Soldiers concentrate on defeating or neutralizing the enemy responsible for causing the injuries. 1-36. During combat, it is crucial to move casualties to a covered and concealed position where first aid can be administered safely. Once the immediate threat subsides, squad leaders should coordinate the evacuation of the wounded to the platoon CCP, typically located to the rear of the platoon's position. At the CCP, the platoon medic will perform triage, stabilize the injured, and initiate their transfer to more comprehensive medical facilities. For detailed operations at the CCP, refer to paragraph 1-20 on page 4. 1-37. Before evacuating casualties to the CCP or further, leaders must ensure that: • The casualty's personal protective equipment, such as protective masks, accompanies them. • All vital operational, sensitive items, and equipment are removed from the casualty. • Medical documentation and identification tags are securely attached to each casualty to streamline medical treatment and tracking processes. 1-38. Additionally, the removal of equipment should include items like automated network control devices, global positioning systems, maps, position-locating devices, and laser pointers. Each unit should have an SOP for managing the weapons and ammunition of its wounded personnel, ensuring these measures are systematically applied, and adhere to safety and operational security standards. 296BKilled in Action 1-39. The platoon leader designates a location for the collection of KIAs. Personal effects remain with the human remains. While treating the human remains with dignity and respect, squad leaders remove, and safeguard all equipment, and government issued items until they can turn the equipment over to the platoon sergeant. The platoon sergeant turns over the human remains to the first sergeant. The platoon should not transport human remains on the same vehicle as wounded Soldiers. The human remains are normally transported to the rear on empty resupply trucks but are dependent on unit SOP.

Casualty Response 23 March 2026 ATP 4-02.11 9 1-40. Commanders and first sergeants establish command procedures to ensure the Soldier’s next of kin are properly notified in accordance with (IAW) ATP 4-46/MCRP 3-40G.3/NTTP 4-06/AFTTP 3-2.51. The potential for unofficial communications exists with the KIA and casualty operations. The use of cell phones and computers in proximity to the area of operation enables many Soldiers to contact their home station regarding the casualty. This kind of communication is unofficial and unacceptable. The next of kin for Soldiers wounded in action or KIA should not receive notification through unofficial means. Therefore, the use of cell phones and computers in proximity to the area of operation should be subject to a communication blackout until the next of kin is notified by a casualty notification officer. No internet or phone calls home should be permitted during the communication blackout. 28BEVACUATION CONSIDERATIONS 1-41. Conducting CASEVAC is a fundamental unit responsibility and a key aspect of sustainment operations. To effectively execute CASEVAC, unit leaders should consider the following points to optimize their planning and response: • Know the Evacuation Platform: ▪ Determine if a medical provider is onboard. ▪ Check for the presence of necessary monitoring equipment. ▪ Ascertain the capacity of the platform regarding how many ambulatory and littler casualties it can evacuate. • Understand Platform Specifications: ▪ Large Platforms: Evacuate multiple casualties, with routine cases loaded first, followed by priority, and critical (urgent) cases last, ensuring they are first off at the destination. ▪ Small Platforms: Prioritize evacuation of critical (urgent) and priority cases first, with routine cases evacuated as space allows. ▪ Verify that all securement devices are functional and appropriate for the type of litter and evacuation platform being used. • Packaging Requirements for the Evacuation Platform: ▪ Identify the types of litters available. ▪ Determine if the litter is stirrup-based verses non-stirrup-based pole-less and is compatible with the evacuation platform. ▪ Ensure there is enough equipment to prevent hypothermia and keep the casualty warm and dry. • Secure the Casualties and Determine the Loading Sequence on the Evacuation Platform: ▪ Implement procedures for tying down or securing litters to the vehicle, ensuring safety during transportation. ▪ Ensure a clear and prioritized loading sequence to streamline the evacuation process. ▪ Plan and coordinate the movement of casualties to the evacuation platform efficiently. 1-42. By addressing these areas and integrating enhancements such as leading in conducting CASEVAC and ensuring all litters are securely tied down, leaders can improve the efficiency and safety of evacuation operations, ultimately enhancing casualty care during critical situations. 297BMedical Evacuation 1-43. A MEDEVAC may be provided by dedicated air or ground ambulances. The MEDEVAC includes the provision of en route medical care, whereas CASEVAC may not provide medical care during movement. For more information on MEDEVAC refer to ATP 4-02.2. If dedicated MEDEVAC platforms (ground and air) are available, casualties should be evacuated on these conveyances to ensure they receive proper en route medical care. If both MEDEVAC and CASEVAC are used, the most seriously injured should be evacuated on MEDEVAC platforms while the less seriously injured are moved by CASEVAC. 1-44. When possible, medical platoon ambulances provide evacuation and en route care from POI or the platoon or company’s CCP to the BAS. The ambulance team supporting the company works in coordination with the senior combat medic supporting the platoons. In mass casualty situations, nonmedical vehicles may be used to assist in CASEVAC as directed by the company commander or leader. However, plans for use of nonmedical vehicles to perform CASEVAC should be included in the unit SOP and briefed at the sustainment and combines arms rehearsals.

Chapter 1 10 ATP 4-02.11 23 March 2026 1-45. When progress of assault units is such that the beachhead is relatively secure, HSS is enhanced from follow-on forces. 317BFollow-on Forces 1-107. The HSS shifts its posture to achieve shore-based health care consistent with the expected combat intensity and duration of sustained operations ashore, independent of sea-based facilities. Timely movement of casualties from the operational environment is important for safety, care for the wounded, and troop morale. Unit leaders are responsible for coordination of CASEVAC from the POI to the appropriate role of care. The owning commands are responsible for CASEVAC from POI or illness to casualty treatment stations, and for casualty movement from the first responder capability to forward resuscitative care (also known as FRC) capabilities. 1-109. CASEVAC can be accomplished through dedicated, designated, or opportune ground or air transportation provided by a combination of litter carries, manual carries, ground transportation, and limited air transport (fixed- or rotary-wing). 1-110. When conducting operations ashore, the patient evacuation team (PET) coordinates patient movement of the patient with requesting unit by ground or air transport or a combination of the two, from POI to the appropriate forward resuscitative care and between various roles of care. The direct air support center and PET receive patient evacuation requests via the 9-line request (see paragraph 3-62 on page 34) over the tactical air request, helicopter request net, or alternate communication means. The PET then determines the appropriate means of patient movement and designated HSS facility. 1-111. If air is the appropriate evacuation means, the direct air support center coordinates air support. If ground evacuation is required or more appropriate, the PET informs the requesting unit to coordinate patient movement with the logistics staff section or logistics combat element. The PET will continue to assist as necessary and track all patient movement through completion of the mission. Depending on the size of the operation, the PET might only assume responsibility for patient movement from POI to forward resuscitative care, and the Marine logistics group HSS medical support operations center or higher regulating authority will assume movement above forward resuscitative care. This should be decided prior to deployment and written into the “Annex Q” (Medical Services) of the operational plan or operation order.

Transportation of casualties away from danger or to evacuation vehicles is a critical aspect of first aid, requiring careful attention to avoid exacerbating injuries. WARNING In cases where a casualty is involved in a vehicle crash, there is a potential for spinal injury. Extraction methods will vary based on mission requirements and vehicle configurations in the operational area. 2-3. Service members should familiarize themselves with safety principles, casualty assessment, and proper training procedures. For instance, if a casualty is on fire, extinguish the flames, address life-threatening bleeding with a tourniquet (TQ) if necessary, and promptly seek cover. 2-4. To remove a casualty laterally from a vehicle— • With the assistance of another Service member, grip the casualty's arms and legs. • Stabilize the casualty's head and neck as much as possible. • Lift them clear of the vehicle and transfer to a safe area on the ground. Note. If available, medical personnel may use a specialized board or splint to stabilize the casualty's head, neck, and upper body. 2-5. To remove a casualty upward from a vehicle— • Use a pistol belt or similar material to encircle the casualty's chest, aiding in their upward movement from the vehicle. • With assistance from another Service member inside the vehicle, elevate the casualty using the pistol belt or by grasping their arms. • While stabilizing the casualty's head and neck as much as possible, lift them free of the vehicle and position them on the topmost side. Note. If medical personnel are present, they may employ a specialized board or splint to stabilize the casualty's head, neck, and upper body. • Depending on the circumstances, relocate the casualty from the topmost side of the vehicle to a secure area on the ground.

Timely evacuation of casualties from the operational environment is crucial not only for their safety and care but also for maintaining troop morale. Squad leaders bear the responsibility for CASEVAC from the POI to the platoon CCP. Casualties with minor wounds might still be able to walk or help carry more seriously injured comrades. Another option is to use a travois or skid, which allows a wounded individual to be strapped on and pulled by one person. Immediate movement may be necessary in certain safety-critical situations, such as a burning vehicle or enemy fire. However, manual carries should not be used for casualties with suspected neck or spine injuries unless there is an immediate life-threatening hazard, and medical advice should be sought. 2-11. Various methods for carrying and dragging litters can be used, depending on the casualty's condition, the terrain, and the level of enemy threat. When planning how to move a casualty, factors to consider include cover and concealment, the weight of the casualty versus the size and strength of the rescuer, nature of the casualty's wounds, the distance to cover, the carrying technique, environmental hazards, and enemy activity. Once a casualty has been treated with a hasty TQ, if the tactical situation allows, priority shifts to getting them to cover and out of enemy fire. Carries and drags enable responders or the CLS to accomplish this swiftly without worsening the casualty's condition. When providing first aid and considering casualty transport, responders must carefully assess the situation, particularly in scenarios like motor vehicle accidents where spinal injuries are a concern. In such cases, moving the casualty may only be advisable if there's an immediate threat to their life, with trained medical personnel ultimately directing transportation decisions. 319BManual Carries 2-13. Manual carries pose physical strain on the bearers and carries the risk of exacerbating the casualty's injuries. However, they can be crucial in saving a casualty's life when other means of transport are unavailable or impractical due to terrain or tactical considerations. Depending on factors such as the bearers' strength and endurance, the casualty's weight, nature of injuries, and obstacles encountered, the distance a casualty can be manually carried varies. Carries can be employed for both conscious and unconscious casualties by one or two bearers. When executed correctly, carries offer the casualty greater protection from additional harm compared to drags and can facilitate movement over longer distances, typically ranging from 50 to 300 meters. For more information on manual carries refer to ATP 4-02.13. 320BDrags 2-14. Drags, on the other hand, are used when swift removal from dangerous or hostile environments is imperative. It's important to exercise caution during casualty handling to avoid causing further harm. For more information on drags refer to ATP 4-02.13. 38BLITTER EVACUATION 2-15. Whenever possible, transporting a casualty on a litter is preferred over manual carries. Litter transport offers greater comfort to the casualty and reduces the risk of worsening their injuries. It facilitates easier and faster evacuation and enables the casualty to be transported over longer distances compared to manual carries. Ideally, a standard litter should be used whenever available. In cases where standard litter is not accessible, an improvised litter can serve as a suitable alternative until the casualty can be transferred to a standard one. It's crucial to ensure that standard litter is always maintained in a serviceable condition. For further guidance on litter evacuation, refer to ATP 4-02.13. 39BEVACUATION PLATFORMS 2-16. In such situations, many vehicles commonly used by units can be repurposed to transport casualties without significant modifications. Units should prioritize planning and training on how their existing vehicles can be used to transport casualties, both with and without litter. Leaders must assess not only their organic platforms but also explore the potential use of civilian, other Services, and coalition platforms. For detailed guidance on evacuation platforms and CASEVAC, refer to ATP 4-02.2, ATP 4-02.13, or STP 8-68W13-SM-TG. 2-17. 23 March 2026 ATP 4-02.11 27 290BPART TWO 293BTACTICAL COMBAT CASUALTY CARE TCCC is crucial for ensuring the safety and health of Service members in combat- related situations. Specifically designed for battlefield conditions, TCCC provides a comprehensive approach to casualty care, focusing on immediate treatment and management. In the fast-paced environment of warfare, adherence to TCCC principles can significantly improve survival outcomes. It equips military units and leaders with the necessary knowledge and skills to provide timely and effective care to injured personnel, thereby reducing fatalities and enhancing survival rates. This publication highlights the vital importance of TCCC in military operations, emphasizing its essential role in saving the lives of Service members and enhancing the overall effectiveness of units. Chapter 3 Fundamentals of Tactical Combat Casualty Care 202BTACTICAL COMBAT CASUALTY CARE OVERVIEW 3-1. In accordance with DODI 1322.24, medical readiness training (also known as MRT) encompasses all facets of medical support across the competition continuum and forms the cornerstone of effective force health protection. TCCC serves as the DOD standard of care for both nonmedical and medical first responders. The TCCC-All Service member course supersedes previous trauma skills taught in self-aid and buddy aid courses, mandating that all Service members receive role-based TCCC training and certification aligned with their assigned skill level as outlined by the JTS. DODI 6040.47 designates the JTS as the DOD’s Center of Excellence for trauma management. 3-2. Service members performing self-aid, buddy aid, and CLS support prioritize their primary combat mission, rendering aid as a secondary mission when feasible. While these roles do not replace the specialized skills of combat medics, corpsmen, and healthcare technicians, they may assist in providing far-forward care and preparing casualties for evacuation if mission and time permit. 3-3. Self-aid, buddy aid, and CLS support are integral components of a comprehensive plan aimed at caring for wounded Service members. A significant advantage of individual Service members providing such support is their proximity to injured squad or crew members. This proximity allows for more immediate care compared to waiting for a combat medic, especially in situations where the medic may be occupied with treating other seriously wounded personnel. First responders and CLS personnel are trained to administer critical immediate care, including addressing severe bleeding and performing needle chest decompression for tension pneumothorax, potentially saving lives in the crucial moments following injury. 203BSERVICE SPECIFIC SKILLS FOR TACTICAL COMBAT CASUALTY CARE 3-4. Individual medical readiness training is built upon a foundation of knowledge, skills, and abilities tailored to operational medicine. DODI 1322.24, published by the JTS, outlines basic TCCC skills

Chapter 3 28 ATP 4-02.11 23 March 2026 for all Service members, allowing individual Services to augment these requirements based on their specific needs. 3-5. TCCC skills are categorized into four tiers, spanning from all Service members to credentialed providers, with each tier building upon the knowledge and skills of the preceding tier. Each tier represents a progression in the complexity and scope of medical interventions, enabling Service members to provide increasingly advanced care to injured personnel. The tiered approach ensures that personnel are trained to the appropriate level based on their roles and responsibilities within their respective units or specialties. 3-6. Tier 1, or All Service member skills, encompasses fundamental skills taught to all Service members, focusing on basic hemorrhage control and recognition of serious injuries. This tier aims to equip every Service member with essential lifesaving capabilities, enabling them to provide immediate care to injured comrades in the battlefield environment. Training in Tier 1 skills is critical for ensuring that all Service members are prepared to respond effectively to medical emergencies, regardless of their primary occupational specialties. 3-7. Tier 2, or CLS skills, involves more advanced care aimed at addressing the most common causes of battlefield fatalities. This tier emphasizes recognizing, preventing, and communicating life-threatening complications to medical personnel. CLS training provides select Service members with enhanced capabilities to stabilize casualties and facilitate their evacuation to higher levels of care, thereby improving overall survival rates in combat environment. 3-8. Tier 3 or Combat Medic and Corpsman skills contains the skills that are much more advanced and focus on invasive care. This tier of skills requires significantly more medical knowledge and skills than self-aid, buddy aid, or CLS. 3-9. Service members and Department of Defense-expeditionary civilian personnel, whether augmentees to operational units or individual augmentees, undergo comprehensive medical readiness training tailored to their deployment circumstances. A profound grasp of TCCC fundamentals can significantly impact outcomes by conserving fighting power, mass, and momentum to support the current fight and potentially saving lives, averting permanent disability, and minimizing hospitalization durations. Emphasizing what actions to take, what to avoid, and when to act. TCCC aims to treat casualties effectively, prevent further harm, and uphold mission completion. Central to TCCC's objectives is addressing and mitigating the causes of preventable death on the battlefield, with training targeting specific areas such as bleeding control, including junctional and noncompressible bleeding, as well as addressing tension pneumothorax and airway complications. 3-35. The TCCC framework encompasses three critical phases of care tailored to the dynamic challenges of battlefield medicine. These phases, structured to address varying levels of urgency and complexity, are Care Under Fire (CUF), Tactical Field Care (TFC), and Tactical Evacuation Care (also known as TACEVAC). Mastery of these phases equips military units and leaders with the proficiency needed to deliver prompt and efficient medical assistance to injured Service members in combat scenarios. Such skills play a pivotal role in preserving life, mitigating the potential for long-term disability, and optimizing the prospects of full recovery for wounded personnel. 43BCARE UNDER FIRE 3-37. Care under fire is the first phase of care in tactical combat casualty care where very limited care is provided for the casualty while the enemy threat is still active. Also known as CUF or care under threat. During CUF, the primary focus is on providing immediate life-saving care while still under enemy fire. This phase involves skills such as returning fire, moving the casualty to a safer location, and controlling severe bleeding using techniques like TQs. The goal is to stabilize the casualty quickly to prevent further injury or death. In CUF, available medical equipment is limited to what is carried by individual responders or casualties, and the only medical priority is addressing massive extremity bleeding due to the ongoing threat in a potentially chaotic and dangerous situation. 3-38. The order of actions during CUF is mission-variable dependent, with scene safety being paramount. For instance, if the threat is suppressed and the tactical situation allows massive life-threatening bleeding and extremity bleeding should be addressed prior to patient movement from the POI. However, each scenario is different, and the ordering of actions could vary accordingly. It's crucial to remember that in the combat environment, there is no "time-out" when casualties occur. Rapid medical and tactical decisions must be made simultaneously, as good medicine can sometimes be bad tactics. Potentially, endangering the lives of responders and jeopardizing the mission's success.

Chapter 3 32 ATP 4-02.11 23 March 2026 3-39. The tactical situation dictates the initial actions during CUF, with little time available for casualty care while under effective enemy fire. Prioritizing suppressing hostile fire and gaining fire superiority is crucial to minimizing the risk of injury to personnel and preventing further harm to the casualty. Wounded Service members should be directed to continue returning fire, moving quickly to nearby cover, and performing self- aid if able. It's essential not to become a casualty oneself, assessing the situation, suppressing enemy fire, and developing a plan before moving to care for a casualty under fire. 3-40. In CUF, early control of severe bleeding is the number one medical priority, as extremity hemorrhage is the most frequent cause of preventable battlefield deaths. Major vessel injuries can quickly lead to shock and death, making it crucial to identify and address life-threatening bleeding promptly. Only massive bleeding warrants intervention during CUF, with treatment of non-life-threatening bleeding deferred until the TFC phase. Despite the grave danger posed by enemy fire, applying a hasty TQ quickly and effectively remains essential in this phase (if this tactical situation allows) to save lives and prevent further casualties. 325BScene Safety 3-41. CUF is defined as the aid rendered at the trauma scene while there is still an active threat. The scene in CUF is never safe, however, the active threat can be reduced. The responder can help others to reduce the threat (return gunfire, or firefighting) and to enable rescuers to reach the casualty and move the casualty to cover. The responder should not risk their personal safety or the safety of the casualty if the threat has not been reduced. 326BControl of Massive Bleeding 3-42. In the CUF phase, the primary focus is on controlling massive bleeding to prevent hypovolemic shock, a critical and potentially fatal condition. Effective management of severe bleeding is essential to stabilize the casualty and ensure survival until further medical treatment can be administered. For detailed strategies and techniques on controlling massive bleeding, see Chapter 4, which provides comprehensive guidance on the procedures and equipment necessary for this vital emergency intervention. 327BCasualty Movement 3-43. If a casualty is unresponsive or unable to move, a rescue plan should be devised and executed if tactically feasible. Do not put two people at risk if it can be avoided. If cover is not available or the wounded Service member cannot move to cover, they should lie flat and motionless. For more information on casualty movement techniques see chapter 2, paragraph 2-6 of this publication. 328BProper Communication and Documentation 3-44. Communication is vital in providing effective care for casualties, involving interaction with the casualty, unit leaders, and on-scene medical personnel. Rescuers should communicate with the casualty as soon as they can safely reach them, by assessing their level of consciousness and orientation. It's crucial to reassure conscious casualties and request assistance from other responders or medics when available, as rescuers are rarely alone in such situations. 3-45. Documentation of all care provided to casualties is essential, primarily utilizing DD Form 1380. This form should include details such as the casualty's name, sex, time of injury, the nature of the injury, along with findings from rapid casualty assessments and the medical aid provided. In the context of CUF, the CLS assumes a role similar to individuals providing self-aid. Extremity hemorrhage, a common cause of preventable combat death, underscores the critical role of TQs in saving lives during CUF scenarios. 3-50. Prompt application of TQs to halt life-threatening bleeding not only saves lives but also enables injured Service members to continue fighting while awaiting further medical care and evacuation. Care provided once the threat has been neutralized, the scene is safe, or the casualty has moved or been moved out of the immediate threat situation. Also known as TFC. However, the tactical situation remains dynamic, and the potential for reverting to a CUF scenario always exists. The primary management plan involves maintaining tactical situational awareness, triaging casualties as needed, and conducting a thorough casualty assessment. 3-53. Mission personnel are tasked with establishing a security perimeter according to unit tactical SOP or battle drills, maintaining security, and remaining vigilant for potential threats from hostile forces. Casualties in shock or under the influence of controlled substances pose risks to themselves and others. Hence, those with altered mental status should have their weapons cleared and secured, communications secured, and sensitive items redistributed. 3-54. During the TFC phase, responders have more time and relatively greater safety to administer further medical care. They may need to continue treatment until medical personnel arrive, assisting them with continued treatment and preparation for evacuation. However, the anticipated time for evacuation to the next level of care may vary based on the operational situation, requiring CLS to remain prepared to reengage the enemy and resume the mission. 3-55. While medical personnel prioritize casualty treatment, coordination between responders and unit leaders is crucial for requesting evacuation assets based on the operational situation. Despite the expanded scope of care in TFC, available medical equipment remains limited to what is carried into the field by the

Tactical evacuation care is the third phase of care in tactical combat casualty care. Care provided during transportation from the battlefield to a medical treatment facility. Tactical evacuation care is the phase of TCCC focused on preparing the casualty for evacuation to a higher role of care, typically an MTF. This phase encompasses both preparing the casualty for evacuation and executing the evacuation process while ensuring continued monitoring and treatment of the casualty's condition. The NATO term of tactical MEDEVAC refers to the intra-theater movement of patients between MTFs within the joint operational area. This process involves transferring patients from one MTF to another using ground, rotary, or fixed-wing assets, along the lines of communication within the joint operational area. In the U.S. Army, this includes MEDEVAC operations between different roles of care, from Role 1 through Role 3, supported by both ground and air ambulances. The proper procedure for performing a 9-line MEDEVAC request is critical in tactical environments to ensure timely evacuation support for casualties. Here's a detailed outline of the steps involved: • Collect Information: Gather all necessary information required for the MEDEVAC request, including the casualty's condition, location, and other pertinent details, using authorized brevity codes. • Initiate Contact: Clearly announce "I HAVE A MEDEVAC REQUEST" over the radio frequency designated for communication with the unit controlling evacuation assets. Wait for one to three seconds for a response. If there is no response, repeat the statement. • Transmit MEDEVAC Request: Contact the unit controlling evacuation assets using the proper call sign and frequency assignment as specified in the signal operating instructions from an automated net control device. • Sequence and Format: Transmit the MEDEVAC information in the proper sequence, stating all line numbers clearly. Line numbers 1 through 5 must be transmitted within 25 seconds during the initial

Lines 6 through 9 can be transmitted while the aircraft or vehicle is en route. • Follow Procedure: Adhere to the procedure provided in the explanation column of the MEDEVAC request format, ensuring all required information is transmitted accurately. • Radio Procedures: Pronounce letters and numbers according to appropriate radio procedures to ensure clarity and understanding. • Use "BREAK": Use "BREAK" on long lines of information to break up the transmission and reduce its length, facilitating better reception. • End Transmission: Conclude the transmission by stating "OVER" to indicate the completion of your message and readiness to receive further instructions or acknowledgment from the evacuation unit. • Maintain Radio Communication: Keep the radio on and listen for additional instructions or contact from the evacuation unit, remaining available for any further communication regarding the MEDEVAC request. 3-63. Prehospital care in the combat setting differs significantly from the civilian setting due to various factors that influence TCCC. These factors include: • Hostile Fire: Combat environments are characterized by the presence of hostile fire, posing an immediate threat to both casualties and responders. This necessitates the integration of tactical considerations into casualty care protocols. • Tactical Considerations: Tactical priorities and objectives often dictate the approach to casualty care. The safety of personnel and the completion of the mission take precedence, influencing how and when medical interventions are performed. • Environmental Considerations: Combat operations can occur in diverse environments, ranging from urban areas to remote and hostile terrain. Responders must adapt their care techniques to address environmental challenges such as extreme weather conditions, limited visibility, and difficult terrain. • Wounding Patterns: In combat, injuries are often caused by explosive devices, firearms, and other weapons unique to warfare. Understanding these specific wounding patterns is crucial for effective casualty management and prioritization of care. • Equipment Constraints: Medical resources and equipment may be limited or unavailable in the combat setting, requiring improvisation and prioritization of essential interventions. Responders must work within the constraints of available resources to provide optimal care. • Delays Reaching Higher Roles of Care: Evacuation to higher levels of care may be delayed in combat situations due to operational factors, such as ongoing enemy engagement or logistical challenges. This necessitates prolonged on-site care and management of casualties by first responders. • Level of First Responder Training and Experience: The training and experience level of first responders, including CLS and medical personnel, significantly impacts the quality and effectiveness of prehospital care in combat. Adequate training ensures responders are proficient in TCCC principles and can adapt to dynamic battlefield conditions. 3-71. 23 March 2026 ATP 4-02.11 43 Chapter 4 Massive Bleeding Control 208BOVERVIEW OF MASSIVE BLEEDING CONTROL 4-1. The number one medical priority in TCCC is early control of severe bleeding. Extremity hemorrhage is the most frequent cause of preventable battlefield deaths. Understanding the human body and how it works along with how casualties survive in combat results in efficient and proper TCCC skills application and an increased survivability of combat casualties. 4-2. Injury to a major blood vessel can quickly lead to shock and death. Only life-threatening extremity bleeding warrants intervention during CUF (if the tactical situation allows). Casualties with injuries to large blood vessels in the extremities (such as the femoral artery in the thigh, or the brachial artery in the upper arm) can result in death in as little as three minutes if bleeding is allowed to continue. If life-threatening bleeding is encountered at the junctional areas (neck, axillary, or inguinal) treatment with a hemostatic dressing is not performed until the casualty transitions to TFC. 4-3. Treatment priorities should follow MARCH-PAWS, with massive bleeding (M) always being the most important. The treatment priorities are not a linear process; if at any time massive bleeding is not controlled, go back to M. 4-4. The initial casualty evaluation should be a rapid head-to-toe check for any unrecognized life-threatening bleeding (a blood sweep). This blood sweep is a systematic way to ensure rapid identification of any unrecognized life-threatening bleeding, and should include a visual and hands-on (palpation) inspection by checking the— • Neck. • Axillary (armpit). • Inguinal (groin). • Legs. • Arms. • Back. 4-5. The priority in caring for a casualty, should be to identify and stop life-threatening bleeding and prevent them from bleeding to death. Bleeding is considered life-threatening when— • There is pulsing or steady bleeding from the wound. • The overlying clothes are soaked with blood. • Blood is pooling on the ground. • There is a traumatic amputation of an extremity. • Bandages or makeshift bandages used to cover the wound are ineffective and are steadily becoming soaked with blood. • There was prior bleeding, and the patient is now in shock (unconscious, confused, and pale). 4-6. A TQ is immediately needed when any of the above examples are present on an extremity. Injury to a major vein or artery can result in shock or death from blood loss in minutes. Extremity (arm or leg) hemorrhage is a leading cause of preventable combat death. Using TQ(s) to stop the bleeding is essential to the survival of casualties with these types of injuries. 4-7. During CUF a TQ is the only medical intervention available to stop life-threatening bleeding from an extremity injury. Airway and other issues are not treated until the TFC phase. 4-8. It may be difficult to determine whether hemorrhage is life-threatening until the TFC phase when the wound can be exposed and evaluated. To effectively perform first aid, Service members need a fundamental understanding of the key body systems, including their structures and functions. Knowledge of the respiratory, circulatory, and musculoskeletal systems is crucial as it helps in assessing injuries and providing the appropriate first aid without causing further harm to the casualty. Familiarity with these systems also aids in recognizing when they are damaged or not functioning properly. Injuries to or compromises of these vital systems can lead to severe, permanent injury or even death. Therefore, a solid grasp of these systems not only supports effective first aid intervention but also helps prevent intensifying the casualty's condition. 54BCIRCULATORY SYSTEM 4-13. The heart and the blood vessels (arteries, veins, and capillaries) circulate blood throughout the body. The heart is divided into two separate halves, each acting as a pump. The left side pumps oxygenated blood (bright red) through the arteries into the capillaries. Nutrients and oxygen pass from the blood through the walls of the capillaries and into the cells. At the same time, waste products and carbon dioxide leave the cells and enter the capillaries. From the capillaries, the blood is carried through the veins to the right side of the heart and then into the lungs where it expels the carbon dioxide and picks up oxygen. Blood in the veins is dark red because of its low oxygen content. Blood does not flow through the veins in spurts as it does through the arteries. The entire system of the heart, blood vessels, and lymphatics is called the circulatory system. 5B LOOD VESSELS 4-14. The body has a complex network of blood vessels that are crucial for blood circulation. These vessels are three main types. First, arteries take oxygen-rich blood from the heart and branch into smaller arterioles, eventually leading to tiny capillaries. Next, capillaries play a key role in exchanging oxygen, nutrients, and wastes between blood and tissues. The blood, now lacking oxygen, moves into small veins called venules, which combine to form larger veins. Lastly, veins are responsible for carrying blood back to the heart, completing the circulation process. 4-15. The blood vessels in the body are all connected and work together. They help deliver oxygen and nutrients to every part of the body and get rid of waste materials. This shows how each type of blood vessel depends on the others, highlighting their important roles in a Service member’s overall health. 56B LOOD 4-16. Blood is a mixture of plasma (liquid component), white blood cells, red blood cells, and platelets. The body contains about 5 to 6 quarts (about 5 liters) of blood. Once blood is pumped out of the heart, it takes 20 to 30 seconds to circulate through the body and return to the heart. 4-17. Blood performs essential functions as it circulates through the body. It delivers oxygen and essential nutrients (such as fats, sugars, minerals, and vitamins) to the body's tissues. It carries carbon dioxide to the lungs and other waste products to the kidneys for elimination from the body. In addition, it carries components that fight infection and stop bleeding.

Massive Bleeding Control 23 March 2026 ATP 4-02.11 45 WARNING If bleeding is not stopped, excessive blood loss can quickly lead to the death of the casualty. It is imperative that first aid providers quickly determine if a casualty is losing blood. Many injuries can result in blood vessels being torn which result in excessive blood loss. 57BHEARTBEAT 4-18. The heart functions as a pump to circulate blood continuously through the blood vessels to all parts of the body. It contracts, forcing the blood from its chambers. The heart then relaxes, permitting its chambers to refill with blood. 4-19. The rhythmical cycle of contraction and relaxation is called the heartbeat. The normal heart rate (heartbeats per minute) varies based on the age and physical condition of the individual at rest. For example— • Adults: 60 to 100 heartbeats per minute. • Children (1 to 6 years): 70 to 120 heartbeats per minute. • Infants (6 to 12 months): 80 to 140 heartbeats per minute. • Infants (0 to 5 months): 90 to 140 heartbeats per minute. Note. The typical pulse for Service members and athletes is 40 to 60 heart beats per minute and is lower than the average adult population due to physical conditioning. 4-20. It is common for a Service member’s pulse to be elevated above the normal range during combat operations as this is both a stressful and high exertional state. Elevated pulse in combination with suspected injuries causing hemorrhage suggests developing shock. 58BPULSE 4-21. The heartbeat causes a rhythmical expansion and contraction of the arteries as it forces blood through them. This cycle of expansion and contraction can be felt (monitored) at various points in the body and is called the pulse. The common points for checking the pulse are at the— • Side of the neck (carotid). • Groin (femoral). • Wrist (radial). • Ankle (posterior tibial). Note. DO NOT use your thumb to check a casualty’s pulse because you may confuse the beat of your own pulse with that of the casualty. WARNING It is imperative that first aid providers quickly determine if the casualty has a pulse (heartbeat). Absence of a pulse (heartbeat) will lead to the death of the casualty if not quickly restored. 4-22. The literature on combat casualty care raises questions about the reliability of traditional blood pressure measurements as indicators of specific pulse types. However, it underscores a crucial reality: as hemorrhage severity increases, more central pulses are likely to be lost, demanding prompt and decisive intervention. Identifying and responding to these central pulses swiftly is imperative in managing severe hemorrhage and ensuring the best possible outcomes for casualties.

Specialized equipment plays a crucial role in effectively managing massive bleeding, offering immediate and life-saving interventions. TQs, junctional tourniquets, hemostatic agents, hemostatic gauze, and pressure dressings, are among the tools used for this purpose. These items form integral components of the TCCC approach to massive bleeding control, empowering military personnel to address severe hemorrhage swiftly and efficiently in the field and enhancing the likelihood of survival for wounded individuals. 59BTOURNIQUETS 4-28. TQs serve as critical devices for halting severe bleeding from extremities, such as arms or legs, by effectively restricting blood flow when applied higher to the injury site, thus preventing further blood loss. 4-29. Considered the most vital lifesaving item in the first aid kit, TQs should be kept easily accessible and ready for use during combat missions. The "TQ, Nonpneumatic Combat Application One-Handed," commonly known as the combat application TQ, is the most prevalent type in military inventory, featuring key components such as the windlass rod for twisting and tightening, a windlass clip to secure the rod, a windlass safety strap for added security, and a routing buckle for TQ band management after looping it around an arm or leg. 4-30. It's imperative that all personnel deployed on combat missions have a CoTCCC recommended TQ readily available in a standard location on their battle gear and are trained in its proper usage. Additionally, casualties should be capable of easily and swiftly accessing and applying their own TQs, emphasizing the importance of not storing TQs at the bottom of the pack, and prioritizing the use of the casualty’s first aid kit TQ first. 60BHEMOSTATIC DRESSING AND WOUND PACKING 4-31. Hemostatic dressings, engineered with clotting agents like kaolin or chitosan, are purpose-built to staunch bleeding efficiently. These dressings are either packed directly into deep or narrow wounds or applied directly onto a bleeding wound, accelerating blood clotting far more effectively than traditional dressings. 4-32. When severe bleeding is noted from a junctional area, such as the neck, axillary or inguinal locations of the body (areas were TQs cannot be applied) hemostatic dressings should be used for massive bleeding control. It's essential to note that they should not be used inside the abdomen or chest, where emergency bandages or other trauma dressings are more appropriate. 4-33. Each first aid kit is typically equipped with one hemostatic dressing and one dry sterile gauze. The hemostatic dressings recommended by the CoTCCC are known to be safe and include active ingredients that help blood to clot at the wound site. Hemostatic dressings are available in various types, one type of hemostatic dressing is impregnated with kaolin, another type contains celox granules, or the third type contains chitosan. Chitosan works by binding red blood cells and platelets to the surface of the dressing, enhancing clot formation. Importantly, despite being derived from shellfish, chitosan does not trigger allergic reactions in individuals with shellfish allergies. 61BPRESSURE DRESSINGS 4-34. Pressure dressings play a crucial role in stemming bleeding by applying direct pressure on wounds. Typically comprised of an elastic bandage and a sterile pad, they are placed over the wound and securely fastened to maintain pressure on the injured area. These dressings not only aid in blood clotting but also compress the open blood vessel, assisting in controlling bleeding effectively. After bleeding has been stemmed with a hemostatic dressing or packing material, it's imperative to maintain pressure on the wound. This is achieved by applying a pressure dressing directly on top of the hemostatic dressing or packing material and wrapping it around the limb, ensuring comprehensive coverage of the wound and gauze applied previously. 4-35. The CoTCCC-recommended emergency bandage or trauma dressing serves as a versatile solution for most wounds, particularly those not severe enough to require a TQ. These dressings can be used alone or in conjunction with other hemorrhage control methods, such as hemostatic gauze and normal gauze, to bolster their effectiveness in controlling bleeding by providing consistent pressure to the wound.

The urgency of promptly stopping massive external bleeding cannot be overstated, as the longer a Service member bleeds from a major wound, the lower their chances of survival become. In combat scenarios, especially while under enemy fire, a TQ stands as the primary means to control massive extremity bleeding, enabling individuals, battle buddies, or combat medics to swiftly manage life- threatening hemorrhages until the casualty can be moved away from the firefight. Always prioritize treating life-threatening hemorrhage while seeking cover. The application of a TQ to a massive bleed is time- sensitive, with the TQ aiming to halt bleeding within one minute and be fully secured within three minutes, casualties with uncontrolled massive bleeding can succumb within these initial minutes. Expecting pain during application is crucial as it signifies proper TQ application. 4-38. The casualty may need to apply a one-handed TQ (see figure 4-5) to an upper extremity when applying self-aid. Regular reassessment of TQ effectiveness is necessary, including checking for stopped bleeding, absent distal pulse, and ensuring no pulse below the TQ on the limb. Common errors when applying TQs include not using one, when necessary, not tightening it adequately, and using it for minimal bleeding. Additionally, TQs should never be removed except by medical personnel at a higher role of care. If the source of massive bleeding is evident, such as from an amputation or major wound, immediate bleeding control measures like applying a TQ or wound packing should be initiated, especially in areas where a TQ cannot be

23 March 2026 ATP 4-02.11 59 Chapter 5 Airway Control 213BOVERVIEW OF AIRWAY CONTROL 5-1. After massive bleeding is controlled, the responder can move on to airway control, the first “A” in the MARCH-PAWS sequence. The casualty must have an open (unobstructed) airway. If the casualty is awake and talking, you can assume the casualty’s airway is open. However, the casualty may still have difficulty breathing. If the casualty is unconscious, their airway must be inspected for any obvious blockages. 5-2. Humans must have oxygen to live. Through the breathing process, the lungs draw oxygen from the air and put it into the blood. The heart pumps the blood through the body to be used by the cells that require a constant supply of oxygen. Some cells are more dependent on a constant supply of oxygen than others. For example, cells of the brain may die within five minutes without oxygen. The brain, heart and lungs are very intolerant to lack of oxygen. The brain is considered one of the organs that is least tolerant to oxygen deprivation. Once these cells die, they are lost forever and do not regenerate. This could result in permanent brain damage, paralysis, or death. 5-3. Airway obstruction on the battlefield is often due to facial trauma. If the casualty is breathing on their own but unconscious or semi-conscious, and there is no airway obstruction, further airway management is achieved through a nasopharyngeal airway (NPA). First responders must assess casualties with facial trauma when contraindications exist to NPA use (such as basilar skull fractures, disruption of the midface, nasopharynx, or roof of the mouth). 5-4. Unconscious casualties can also lose their airway as the muscles of their tongue may have relaxed. This causes the tongue to block the airway by sliding to the back of the mouth and covering the opening to the windpipe. The signs and symptoms of airway obstruction include: • Casualty is in distress and indicating that they cannot breathe properly. • Casualty making snoring or gurgling sounds. • Visible blood or foreign objects are present in the airway. • Severe trauma to the face is observed. 73BRESPIRATION 5-5. Respiration is the process where we breathe in oxygen and breathe out carbon dioxide. The efficiency of this process can vary depending on someone's age and physical health. Generally, adults breathe 12 to 20 times a minute. But children and infants have different rates. For instance, children aged one to 10 years take 15 to 30 breaths per minute. Infants who are six to 12 months old breath faster, at a rate of 25 to 50 times per minute. Meanwhile, the youngest infants, those aged zero to five months, have a rate of 25 to 40 breaths per minute. 74BANATOMY AND PHYSIOLOGY OF THE RESPIRATORY SYSTEM 5-6. The respiratory system consists of the airway, lungs, and rib cage. The airway consists of the nose, mouth, throat, voice box, and windpipe. Air passes to and from the lungs through the canal. The lungs are two elastic organs made up of thousands of tiny air spaces or sacs and covered by an airtight membrane. The bronchial tree is a part of the lungs. The rib cage is the structure that joins the spine in the back and the breastbone in front, which protects the heart and lungs. The top part of the rib cage is closed by the structure of the neck, and the bottom part is separated from the abdominal cavity by a large dome-shaped muscle called the diaphragm (figure 5-1 on page 60).

Chapter 5 60 ATP 4-02.11 23 March 2026 Figure 5-1. Airway, lungs, and the rib cage 5-7. The diaphragm and rib muscles, which are under the control of the respiratory center in the brain, automatically contract and relax. Inspiration increases and expiration decreases the size of the rib cage. When the rib cage increases and then decreases, the air pressure in the lungs is first less and then more than the atmospheric pressure, thus causing the air to rush into and out of the lungs to equalize the pressure. 214BEQUIPMENT USED FOR AIRWAY CONTROL 5-8. The CoTCCC-recommended NPA with lubricant is a nonsterile, rubber tube-shaped device that is inserted into the nostril of a casualty. It acts as a wedge to keep the airway open by keeping the tongue from falling back into the space behind the mouth leading to the windpipe. Only an NPA, size 32 French, is found within the standard issued JFAKs. Sizing the NPA before insertion is not necessary but is important to minimize nasopharyngeal trauma or elicit the casualty’s gag reflex. The lubricant is a water-based substance that assists in inserting the device into the nose. Use of an NPA is a Tier 2 skill. CAUTION Do NOT use blood or other body fluids to lubricate the NPA. 215BTIER 1 SKILLS FOR AIRWAY CONTROL 5-9.
