External chest compressions, also known as Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (CPR), in combat casualties is nearly always the result of hemorrhagic or obstructive shock, neither of which will respond to standard CPR. Conducting CPR may delay definitive treatment in nearly all cases. The CoTCCC guidelines recommend performing bilateral needle decompression and expedite blood product administration. Mission variables or the credentialed provider may guide exceptions to this rule in support of CPR on combat casualties. The administration of CPR on a combat casualty should be a rare circumstance and not the standard of care in this trauma population. 6-45. CPR is conducted using a specific technique to provide manual circulation support during cardiac arrest or when the heart has stopped beating effectively. A general outline of the steps involved in conducting external chest compressions is: • Position: Ensure the person is lying on a firm, flat surface, such as the ground or a CPR board. Kneel beside the person's chest.

Respiration and Breathing Control 23 March 2026 ATP 4-02.11 81 • Hand Placement: Place the heel of one hand on the center of the person's chest, between the nipples. For infants or children, use two or three fingers instead of the entire hand. • Compression Depth: Press down firmly and smoothly. For adults, compress the chest at least two inches (five centimeters) deep. For infants or children, compress the chest about one-third to one- half of its depth. • Compression Rate: Perform compressions at a rate of 100 to 120 compressions per minute. This equates to about two compressions per second. • Complete Chest Recoil: Allow the chest to fully recoil between each compression, without lifting your hands off the chest. This allows the heart to refill with blood. • Compression to Ventilation Ratio: If you are performing CPR alone, do cycles of 30 chest compressions to two rescue breaths (mouth-to-mouth or mouth-to-mask). If there are two rescuers, the ratio can be 30:2 or continuous chest compressions with ventilation being delivered by the other rescuer. • Continue until Help Arrives: Keep performing chest compressions until professional medical help arrives, or until the person shows signs of movement or starts breathing. 6-46. It is important to note that these steps provide a general overview of external chest compressions. Proper CPR training and certification are needed to gain a thorough understanding of the technique and to ensure accurate and effective application during emergency situations. 6-47. The duration of CPR can vary depending on the circumstances and response of the individual being treated. In general, CPR should be continued until one of the following conditions is met: • Signs of Life: If the person shows obvious signs of life, such as breathing normally, coughing, or moving, CPR can be stopped. • Professional Medical Help Arrives: CPR should be continued until professional medical personnel take over the resuscitation efforts. • Provider Fatigue: If the person performing CPR becomes too exhausted to continue effectively, they can switch with another trained individual to maintain the quality of compression. 6-48. In many cases, CPR is performed continuously without interruptions until one of the above conditions is met. However, it is important to note that high-quality chest compressions are crucial for improving the chances of survival. Rescue breathing, also known as artificial ventilation, is a technique used in CPR to provide oxygen to a person who is not breathing or has inadequate breathing. It involves delivering breaths into the person's lungs to support their respiratory function. Rescue breathing is conducted executing the following: • Position: Ensure the casualty is lying on a flat surface, preferably with their head tilted back slightly to open the airway. • Clear the Airway: Check for any visible obstructions in the person's mouth or throat, and if present, gently remove them if possible. • Seal the Mouth: If the casualty's mouth is open, use your hand to gently lift the chin upward to maintain an open airway. With your other hand, pinch the person's nose closed to prevent air from escaping. • Breathing Technique: Place your mouth over the casualty's mouth, forming a seal, and blow into their mouth while watching for the chest to rise. Deliver the breath over one second and make sure it is sufficient to visibly inflate the chest. • Breathing Rate: Provide rescue breaths at a rate of about one breath every five to six seconds (10 to 12 breaths per minute). • Chest Recoil: Allow the chest to fully recoil between breaths. This enables the chest to return to its resting position, which helps in the exchange of gases during respiration. • Continue Until Help Arrives: Perform rescue breathing until professional medical help arrives or until the person starts breathing on their own. 6-50. Chapter 6 82 ATP 4-02.11 23 March 2026 • Mouth-to-Mouth: This common method involves the rescuer forming a seal over the casualty's mouth with their own and delivering breaths into their lungs. • Mouth-to-Nose: Used when the casualty's mouth is injured, obstructed, or inaccessible, the rescuer closes the casualty's mouth and breathes into their nose to create a seal. • Mouth-to-Mask: In situations like professional CPR or with specialized equipment, a pocket mask or BVM device is used. Controlling shock is the primary method of circulation control. Shock is the inadequate blood flow to body tissues. Inadequate blood volume inside the circulatory system results in inadequate oxygen delivery to the body’s cells. As cells, tissues, and organs cease to function, eventually the whole body will fail, and death follows. Note. Hypovolemic shock can also result from blood loss due to internal bleeding into the abdominal or chest cavity. The first responder or CLS will not be able to control internal bleeding. This condition requires rapid evacuation of the casualty. 7-5. Shock is caused by a decrease in the amount of blood volume circulating in the casualty's blood circulatory system. Shock is usually caused by severe bleeding, but it can also be caused by severe burns classified as partial thickness burns (2nd degree) or full thickness burns (3rd degree) on 20 percent or more of the body surface. On the battlefield, assume shock is from severe blood loss (also called hemorrhagic shock). The signs and symptoms of shock include: • Mental confusion. • Weak or absent radial pulse. • Rapid breathing. • Nausea. • Sweaty, cool, or clammy skin. • Excessive thirst. • Pale or gray skin. • Previous severe bleeding

Anaphylactic shock is a severe and life-threatening allergic reaction that significantly impacts the circulatory system. This medical emergency is marked by a swift release of histamines and other chemicals into the body, leading to vasodilation and increased permeability in blood vessels. Further doses of epinephrine may be necessary, administered every 5 to 10 minutes if prescribed and symptoms persist. Record all first aid actions on DD Form 1380 and request MEDEVAC immediately. Use CASEVAC only if MEDEVAC is unavailable and transport the casualty to the nearest MTF as soon as possible. 23 March 2026 ATP 4-02.11 89 Chapter 8 Hypothermia Control 28BOVERVIEW OF HYPOTHERMIA CONTROL 8-1. The “H” in MARCH-PAWS stands for hypothermia prevention. Hypothermia begins when the body’s core temperature drops below 97° Fahrenheit (F). It can be mild (93-96°F), moderate (89-93°F), or severe (less than 89°F), depending on the temperature. To accurately diagnose hypothermia, the core temperature must be measured rectally with a special low-range thermometer, as mouth and ear measurements won't work well in cold environments. 8-2. Hypothermia can be caused by being in a cold environment or by losing a lot of blood, a condition known as hypovolemia. This is when there’s a significant drop in the volume of blood circulating in the body. Both environmental exposure and loss of blood can lead to dangerously low body temperatures, which can be life-threatening if not treated. 8-3. Environmental hypothermia happens when the body loses heat faster than it can produce it, often from being in cold weather for too long. Hypothermia from hypovolemic shock happens due to a large loss of blood or fluids, making it hard for the body to keep warm. Both causes can lead to serious health issues, including death, if not managed quickly. 8-4. Hypothermia can happen suddenly, like from falling into cold water, or slowly, if someone is exposed to cold conditions for a long time. It can even happen in mild temperatures if a person is wet, which makes it easier to lose body heat. Factors like wet clothing, not enough food, exhaustion, and drinking alcohol or using drugs can make hypothermia worse. 8-5. Massive bleeding can cause hypothermia, which in turn can cause more bleeding because cold temperatures can prevent blood from clotting properly. This is a problem even in warm weather, and especially for people in shock who can’t generate enough body heat. It’s crucial to stop this cycle to save the person’s life. 96BSIGNS AND SYMPTOMS OF HYPOTHERMIA 8-6. In the TFC phase of care, the focus has shifted from immediate life-threatening hemorrhage control during CUF phase, to the reassessment of all previous interventions. This is followed by the prevention and treatment of other injuries and complications such as hypothermia. It is important to identify the signs of hypothermia. Some easily recognizable signs of hypothermia are: • Vigorous shivering is typically present. • Shivering may decrease or cease as the core temperature continues to fall. • Conscious, but usually apathetic or lethargic. • Confusion. • Sleepiness. • Slurred speech or mumbling. • Slow breathing and drowsiness. • Weak pulse. • Low or unattainable blood pressure. • Change in behavior with or without poor control over body movements, and with or without slow reactions. 8-7. The signs and symptoms of hypothermia may vary depending on the severity and can be categorized into mild, moderate, and severe stages: • Mild Hypothermia: ▪ Shivering. ▪ Cold and pale skin. ▪ Numbness or tingling in extremities. ▪ Fatigue and drowsiness.

Chapter 8 90 ATP 4-02.11 23 March 2026 ▪ Slurred speech. ▪ Impaired coordination and fine motor skills. • Moderate Hypothermia: ▪ Intense shivering or shivering stops. ▪ Difficulty in speaking and thinking clearly. ▪ Clumsiness and lack of coordination. ▪ Cold, pale, or blue-gray skin. ▪ Slow breathing and heart rate. ▪ Weak pulse. • Severe Hypothermia: ▪ Shivering may stop completely. ▪ Confusion and disorientation. ▪ Loss of consciousness. ▪ Very cold, pale, or bluish skin. ▪ Slow or irregular breathing. ▪ Weak or absent pulse. 97BFIRST AID FOR HYPOTHERMIA 8-8. Re-warming techniques include— • Remove the casualty from the cold environment. • Replace wet clothing with dry clothing. • Cover the casualty with insulating material or blanket. • Wrap the casualty from head to toe. • Avoid unnecessary movement from the casualty. • If the casualty is conscious, slowly give high caloric sweet warm fluids. • Seek medical aid. 8-10. 23 March 2026 ATP 4-02.11 107 Chapter 11 Head Injury 239BOVERVIEW OF HEAD INJURIES 11-1. Head injuries are a common concern that can occur due to accidents, falls, or sports-related incidents. When the head experiences a forceful impact, it can result in different types of injuries. Understanding head injuries can help Service members take the necessary precautions to protect themselves or others from potential harm. It is critically important to report findings of a head injury to medical personnel at the scene since a lack of rapid, and appropriate medical care can worsen the head injury, and the eventual outcome. Head trauma can be either blunt or penetrating. Head injuries can be broadly classified as open or closed head injuries. 108BOPEN HEAD INJURY 11-2. An open head injury, also known as an open skull injury, is a type of injury that occurs when there is a break or penetration of the skull, exposing the brain to the external environment. It typically involves visible damage to the scalp, skull, or meninges (protective coverings of the brain). The signs and symptoms of an open head injury can vary depending on the severity and specific location of the injury. Open head injuries are considered medical emergencies. If an open head injury is suspected, it is crucial to seek immediate medical attention for evaluation, diagnosis, and appropriate treatment. 11-3. The common signs and symptoms associated with an open head injury are: • Visible head wound. An open head injury often involves a visible wound or laceration on the scalp or skull. There may be bleeding, or an open fracture where the bone is exposed. • Profuse bleeding. Open head injuries can cause significant bleeding due to damage to blood vessels. Blood may be visible on the scalp, face, or in severe cases, there may be profuse bleeding from the head wound. • Skull deformity. In some cases, an open head injury may cause a visible deformity or depression in the skull, indicating a skull fracture or bone displacement. • Loss of consciousness. Depending on the severity of the injury, loss of consciousness can occur, ranging from a brief period to an extended duration. • Clear fluid or blood drainage. Leakage of clear fluid (cerebrospinal fluid) or blood from the nose, ears, or wound can indicate a more severe injury and should be treated as an emergency. • Severe headache. An intense and persistent headache is common following an open head injury. • Nausea and vomiting. Feelings of nausea and vomiting may be present after an open head injury. • Confusion and disorientation. The Service member may exhibit confusion, memory loss, difficulty concentrating, or may appear disoriented. • Seizures. Seizures can occur after an open head injury, especially if the brain is directly affected. • Changes in speech or vision. The person may have difficulties with speech, vision problems, double vision, or other sensory disturbances. • Weaknesses or numbness. Weakness or numbness in certain body parts can be a sign of nerve damage resulting from the head injury. 109BCLOSED HEAD INJURY 11-4. A closed head injury refers to trauma to the head that does not involve an open wound or penetration of the skull. Instead, the injury occurs internally, within the skull. Closed head injuries are often the result of blunt force impacts, falls, or accidents, where the brain is subjected to sudden acceleration, deceleration, or rotational forces. Concussions are the most common type of a closed head injury. Closed head injuries may not be obvious or detectable. 11-5. Closed head injuries can range in severity from mild concussions to more severe forms, such as contusions, diffuse axonal injuries, or intracranial hemorrhages. It is essential to seek medical attention if a

Chapter 11 108 ATP 4-02.11 23 March 2026 closed head injury is suspected, as the impact on the brain can have serious consequences and requires appropriate evaluation and management. 11-6. The signs and symptoms of a closed head injury can vary depending on the severity of the injury. Mild cases may be present with subtle symptoms, while more severe injuries can have immediate and pronounced effects. The common signs and symptoms associated with a closed head injury are: • Headache or pressure in the head. • Nausea and vomiting. • Dizziness and balance problems. • Confusion and disorientation. • Memory loss or difficulty concentrating. • Mood and behavior changes. • Sensory changes, such as blurred vision, or ringing in the ears. • Sensitivity to light and sound. • Loss of consciousness (in severe cases). 11-7. It is important to seek medical attention if any of these signs are present after a head injury, as they can indicate a range of severity from a mild concussion to more serious brain trauma. The above symptoms can occur immediately after the injury or may develop gradually over time. Symptoms may vary from person to person. 10BCONCUSSIONS 11-8. A concussion is a type of traumatic brain injury that occurs when the brain experiences a sudden and forceful movement within the skull. It is typically caused by a blow, jolt, or bump to the head or body, which can disrupt the normal functioning of the brain. 11-9. Concussions can occur in various situations, such as sports-related injuries, falls, motor vehicle accidents, or any other incident involving a significant impact to the head. Concussions can happen even without a direct impact to the head. The forceful movement or shaking of the body can still cause the brain to move inside the skull, leading to a concussion. 11-10. The primary characteristic of a concussion is a temporary disruption of brain function. Concussions may not always involve a loss of consciousness. In fact, most concussions occur without a person losing consciousness. Common symptoms of a concussion can include: • Headache or pressure in the head. • Dizziness or feeling lightheaded. • Confusion or feeling mentally foggy. • Memory problems or difficulty concentrating. • Fatigue or feeling tired. • Nausea or vomiting. • Sensitivity to light or noise. • Changes in sleep patterns. • Irritability or changes in mood. • Blurred vision or difficulty with balance. 11-11. It’s important to seek medical attention if a concussion is suspected, as health care professionals can evaluate the severity of the injury and provide appropriate guidance for recovery. The initial management of a concussion involves rest and avoiding activities that could further injure the brain. Physical and cognitive rest are recommended to allow the brain to heal properly. In some cases, individuals may need to temporarily limit activities like school or work to promote recovery. A gradual return to normal activities is typically recommended under the guidance of a health care professional. 11-12. Every concussion is unique, and the symptoms and recovery time can vary from person to person. With proper rest, most individuals recover fully from a concussion. However, in some cases, symptoms may persist or worsen, and a condition known as post-concussion syndrome may develop.

Head Injury 23 March 2026 ATP 4-02.11 109 1BCONTUSIONS RELATED TO HEAD INJURIES 11-13. A contusion refers to a type of injury characterized by damage to the tissue or blood vessels beneath the skin, usually resulting from a blunt force impact. It is commonly known as a bruise. When a contusion occurs, blood vessels are damaged, leading to bleeding and the subsequent discoloration of the skin. 11-14. In relation to head injuries, contusions can occur because of a direct blow or trauma to the head. When the head experiences a significant impact, the brain can collide with the inner surface of the skull, leading to contusions. These types of injuries are known as cerebral contusions. 11-15. Cerebral contusions can be classified as coup-contrecoup injuries, which means that contusions can occur both at the site of impact (coup) and on the opposite side of the brain due to the brain rebounding and hitting the skull (contrecoup). These injuries are concerning because they involve damage to the brain tissue itself. 11-16. The severity of a cerebral contusion can vary, ranging from mild to severe. In more severe cases, contusions can lead to increased pressure within the skull, swelling of the brain, and potentially life- threatening complications. 11-17. It is crucial to seek immediate medical attention if a head injury is suspected, as prompt evaluation and treatment are essential to prevent further complications. Symptoms of a cerebral contusion may include: • Changes in vision. • Confusion. • Difficulty speaking. • Dizziness. • Headache. • Loss of consciousness. • Nausea. • Seizures. • Vomiting. • Weaknesses. 11-18. Treatment for cerebral contusions focuses on managing the underlying injury and preventing further damage. It may involve measures such as rest, pain management, observation, close monitoring of neurological status, and, in more severe cases, surgical intervention to relieve pressure and remove any blood clots or damaged tissue. 240BEQUIPMENT USED FOR THE TREATMENT OF A HEAD INJURY 11-19. Sterile gauze pads or clean clothes are vital for covering and applying pressure to the wound to stop the bleeding. Adhesive bandages or medical tape are used to secure the gauze in place. Additionally, a mild antiseptic solution or wipes are important for cleaning the wound to prevent infection. Lastly, a cravat or gauze bandage can be used to create a makeshift dressing or sling to support the head if there is a suspected skull or neck injury. 241BTIER 1 SKILLS FOR THE TREATMENT OF A HEAD INJURY 11-20. Head Injury 23 March 2026 ATP 4-02.11 111 11-28. Prompt first aid measures should be initiated for casualties with suspected head and neck injuries. The conscious casualty may be able to provide information on the extent of their injuries. However, because of the head injury, they may be confused and unable to provide accurate information. Do they know where they are? When encountering an unconscious casualty, it is essential to act swiftly and methodically, as their condition may be critical. Unconsciousness can result from various causes, such as trauma, medical emergencies, or underlying health conditions. The primary objective of first aid for an unconscious patient is to ensure their immediate safety, preserve their airway, and seek professional medical help. By following specific guidelines and employing basic life support techniques, first responders can play a vital role in providing initial assistance until medical professionals arrive. An unconscious casualty does not have control of all their functions and may choke on their tongue, blood, vomitus, or other substances resulting in: • Loss of Breathing. The brain requires a constant supply of oxygen. A bluish (or an individual with dark skin-grayish) color of skin around the lips and nail beds indicates that the casualty is not receiving enough oxygen. Immediate action must be taken to clear the airway, to position the casualty on their side, or to initiate rescue breathing. • Bleeding. Bleeding from a head injury usually comes from blood vessels within the scalp. Bleeding can also develop inside the skull or within the brain. In most instances visible bleeding from the head can be controlled by application of the field first aid dressing. CAUTION DO NOT attempt to put unnecessary pressure on the wound or attempt to push any brain matter back into the head (skull). DO NOT apply pressure dressing. • Convulsions. Convulsions (seizures or involuntary jerking) may occur even after a mild head injury. When a casualty is convulsing, protect them from hurting themselves. Take the following measures: ▪ Ease them to the ground if they are standing or sitting. ▪ Support their head and neck. ▪ Maintain their airway. ▪ Protect them from further injury (such as hitting close-by objects). Note. DO NOT forcefully hold their arms and legs if they are jerking because this can lead to broken bones. DO NOT force anything between the casualties’ teeth-especially if they are tightly clenched because this may obstruct the casualty’s airway. Maintain the casualty’s airway if necessary.

23 March 2026 ATP 4-02.11 115 Chapter 12 Burns 24BOVERVIEW OF BURNS 12-1. A burned trauma casualty should be treated for all other life-threatening injuries first, following the MARCH-PAWS sequence, before addressing burns. Even if the skin is burned, trauma treatments can still be performed on or through it. 12-2. Burns can result from various causes: • Friction Burns. These are common in situations where skin is rubbed off against a hard surface, often seen in road accidents where motorcycle riders, cyclists, or skateboarders slide across pavement, getting what's known as "road rash." Carpet burns occur from skin scraping against carpet, often during indoor sports or play. Rope burns are common during activities like climbing or tug-of-war, and sliding burns frequently happen in sports like baseball when sliding into bases. • Cold Burns. Also known as frostbite, these burns damage the skin by freezing it. Frostbite can occur from prolonged exposure to freezing temperatures or direct contact with extremely cold objects. • Thermal Burns. These occur when the skin touches something very hot, like hot metals, scalding liquids, flames, or steam, raising the skin temperature high enough to kill skin cells. • Radiation Burns. Sunburn is a typical example. Other sources include X-rays or radiation therapy for cancer. • Chemical Burns. These happen when strong acids, solvents, or detergents come into contact with the skin. • Electrical Burns. These burns are the result of contact with electrical currents. 12-3. Burns are classified based on how deeply they damage the skin: • Superficial or First Degree Burns (figure 12-1 on page 116): Superficial burns affect only the outer layer of the skin, causing redness, pain, and mild swelling. They are like mild sunburn and usually heal within a few days without leaving scars. • Partial thickness or Second Degree Burns (figure 12-2 on page 116): Partial thickness burns reach the second layer of the skin and can cause blisters, severe pain, redness, and swelling. Healing times vary, and these burns may leave scars. • Full thickness or Third Degree Burns (figure 12-3 on page 116): Full thickness burns are the most severe, these burns go through the entire thickness of the skin and can damage muscles or bones underneath. The skin may look white, blackened, or charred, and there might be no feeling in the area because of nerve damage. These burns require immediate medical attention and often need skin grafts to heal.

The CoTCCC-recommended compressed gauze and or gauze rolls are 6-ply sterile cotton that has been compressed. They are used to stop minor bleeding, cover wounds or burns, pack wounds, act as bulky material for pressure dressings, or pad pressure points in splinting. 12-7. The CoTCCC-recommended elastic bandage is a stretchable bandage. They are used to hold dressings or splints in place or can be applied more tightly to apply localized pressure on a wound. Elastic or restrictive bandages are normally not applied to a burn casualty. The application of these types of bandages are very painful and swelling secondary to the injury may restrict circulation. 12-8. The cravat is a sterile triangular shaped bandage. It can be used as both a bandage and a sling. It is commonly used to secure a splint, create a sling, or swath for an injured limb. 246BTIER 1 SKILLS FOR THE TREATMENT OF BURNS 12-9. Burn care in TCCC is very basic. Eliminating the source of the burn should be the initial priority. Providing any treatment prior to removing the casualty from the source of the burn or extinguishing the cause of the burn will be ineffective and harmful to the casualty and casualty response personnel. 12-10. Electrical burn care consists of— • Eliminating the source of electrical burns. • Turning off any sources of electricity that have been exposed to the casualty (if applicable). • Using nonconductive material to drag the casualty away from the electrical source (if it cannot be turned off). Note. Types of nonconductive material include rope, clothing, and dry wood. • Moving the casualty to a safe place. WARNING Do not touch the casualty or the electrical source with your bare hands. You will be injured too! High voltage electrical burns from an electrical source or lightning may cause temporary unconsciousness, difficulties in breathing, or difficulties with the heart (irregular heartbeat). 12-11. Thermal burn care consists of— • Stopping the source of the thermal burn and remove the casualty from the source of the burn. • Extinguishing any flames on the casualty, cut the clothing around the burned area, and gently lift away. CAUTION If clothing is stuck to the burn, ensure you cut around the clothing and leave the stuck clothing in place.

Chapter 12 118 ATP 4-02.11 23 March 2026 • Avoid grabbing the burned area while moving or picking up the casualty. 12-12. Chemical burn care consists of— • Eliminating the source of chemical burns. • Brushing off dry chemicals (carefully) with a clean, dry cloth. • Flush the burned area with copious amounts of flowing water to remove any liquid chemicals. • Applying a wet barrier (water-soaked gauze, clothing, or mud) with an occlusive dressing. • Advising medical personnel immediately. WARNING Do not submerge a chemical burn casualty in water. This will greatly contribute to hypothermia and spread the irritation. 12-13. All burn care consists of— • Monitoring the casualty for life-threatening conditions. • Checking for additional injuries. • Treating for shock (if applicable). • Seeking medical aid. • Annotating all treatment and care on DD Form 1380. 12-14. Close attention to the casualty’s airway, breathing is required and always assess for secondary injuries and shock. 247BTIER 2 SKILLS FOR THE TREATMENT OF BURNS 12-15. Along with the treatment measures outlined in paragraph 13-9 through 13-14 extra emphasis should be placed on heat loss prevention methods. Burn patients are particularly susceptible to hypothermia. Casualties should be kept off the ground and placed onto an insulated surface as soon as possible. 12-16. For extensive burns, those with greater than 20 percent of the area burned place the casualty in the Heat Reflective Shield to cover the burned areas and prevent hypothermia. Preventing and managing hypothermia for burn patients is important and occurs regardless of the ambient temperature in the environment. 12-17. Facial burns, especially those that occur in closed spaces, may be associated with an inhalation injury. These casualties should be monitored closely for potential airway issues. Do not place an NPA in a casualty with signs of inhalation burns. Notify medical personnel as soon as possible if an inhalation injury is suspected. 12-18. Analgesia may be administered to treat burn pain. Antibiotic therapy is not solely indicated for burns; it should also be given to prevent infection in penetrating wounds. Consider giving the entire combat pill pack if medical treatment takes more than three hours from the time of injury, and if giving the medication to the casualty does not cause nausea. 12-19. Interventions for warm and cool weather should be considered. The addition of blood loss can cause the body’s temperature to drop even when it is hot outside. The TQs should not be covered; keep them visible so medical personnel can easily see it. 248BEXPEDIENT SKILLS USED FOR THE TREATMENT OF BURNS 12-20. In emergency scenarios, especially in remote or combat zones, effectively managing burn injuries with limited resources is essential. Basic materials such as gauze bandage, clean clothing, and cravats can be used to cover burns and control bleeding. Cooling and cleaning burns should be done with available clean water, avoiding ice to prevent further skin damage. For thermal burns, it's crucial to remove the casualty from the heat source and cut away clothing gently around the burn area. In cases of electrical burns, disconnecting the power and using non-conductive materials to move the casualty is vital, while chemical burns require immediate decontamination by brushing off dry chemicals and flushing the area thoroughly with water.

Burns 23 March 2026 ATP 4-02.11 119 12-21. Preventing hypothermia is critical in burn care due to the high risk posed by skin damage. Using emergency blankets, reflective heat shields, or makeshift insulation from natural materials can help maintain body temperature. Pain management, when possible, should include safe administration of over-the-counter pain relievers, and continuous monitoring for shock is essential. These field expedient techniques are pivotal in stabilizing burn victims and preventing further injury until more advanced medical help can be accessed, underscoring the importance of training and preparedness in these emergency interventions.

23 March 2026 ATP 4-02.11 121 Chapter 13 Fractures and Splinting 249BOVERVIEW OF FRACTURES 13-1. Prompt and appropriate management of fractures, or breaks in bones, is essential to minimize further harm and optimize the chances of survival for injured individuals. TCCC emphasizes a systematic approach to fracture care, incorporating principles such as rapid assessment, stabilization, and pain management. The goal is to provide efficient and effective treatment, considering the challenges of the tactical environment where resources may be limited, and evacuation to definitive care may be delayed. Mastery of fracture management in TCCC equips military personnel and first responders with the skills necessary to stabilize fractures, prevent complications, and facilitate the evacuation process, ultimately improving the overall outcomes for casualties in the field. 16BMUSCULOSKELETAL SYSTEM 13-2. The musculoskeletal system provides a structural framework for the body and, because bones are rigid, provides support and protection for vital organs and softer tissues. Skeletal muscles and bones work together to make body movement possible. 13-3. The musculoskeletal system is composed of— • Bones. • Joints. • Muscles. • Cartilage. • Ligaments. • Tendons. 360B ones 13-4. Bones are the substance that forms the skeleton of the body. It is composed chiefly of calcium phosphate and calcium carbonate. The human body has 206 bones. There are 80 axial (head and trunk) bones and 126 appendicular (upper and lower extremity) bones. Bones provide structural support for the body. Individual and groups of bones provide structure for the attachment of soft tissues and protect organs. 361BJoints 13-5. The human body's mobility hinges on its joints, where bones connect and facilitate movement. These pivotal junctures come in various forms, each serving distinct functions in enabling motion. 362BMuscles 13-6. The body's muscles serve as its powerhouse, providing the force needed for movement and various physiological functions. Within the body, there exist three main types of muscles, each with its unique roles and characteristics. These include skeletal muscles, which control movement in the extremities and outer body areas, cardiac muscles, found exclusively in the heart, and smooth muscles, lining the walls of arteries and the gastrointestinal tract. 363BCartilage 13-7. Cartilage serves as a resilient and pliable tissue that provides cushioning and support between bones at the joints, facilitating smooth movement. In addition to its role in joint function, cartilage also forms essential structures elsewhere in the body, such as the larynx and the external portions of the ears, contributing to their flexibility and shape.

Chapter 13 122 ATP 4-02.11 23 March 2026 364BLigaments 13-8. Ligaments play a crucial role in the body's structural integrity, serving as sturdy bands of connective tissue that link bones together at joints. They provide stability and support, helping to prevent excessive movement and potential joint injuries. 365BTendons 13-9. Tendons serve as soft tissue connectors that attach muscles to bones, enabling movement and transmitting the force generated by muscles to the bones they are connected to. Despite their flexibility, tendons possess considerable toughness, providing durability to withstand the stresses of movement and physical activity. 17BTYPES OF FRACTURES 13-10. A fracture can be a closed or open fracture. A closed fracture (see figure 13-1) means that there is no external wound associated with the fracture. An open fracture (see figure 13-2) means that there is a break in the skin in conjunction with the fracture, often with protruding bone. The warning signs that an arm or leg might be fractured include: • Significant pain along with marked swelling. • An audible or perceived “snap.” • Different length or shape of limb. • Loss of pulse or sensation in the injured arm or leg. • Crepitus (a crackling or popping sound under the skin). The CoTCCC endorses the use of the semi-rigid splint, a 36-inch-long malleable device comprised of moldable aluminum, encased in foam padding. This type of splint is designed for versatility in the field and is most commonly employed for stabilizing fractures. Its flexible yet sturdy structure allows it to be shaped according to the specific contours of the injury site, providing effective support and immobilization needed to prevent further injury during transport or until more definitive care can be administered.

Fractures and Splinting 23 March 2026 ATP 4-02.11 123 251BTIER 1 SKILLS FOR THE TREATMENT OF FRACTURES 13-12. During the TFC phase, it is highly advisable to splint all fractures if circumstances permit. Splinting is crucial to immobilize the affected area, preventing further damage, and minimizing pain for the casualty. Proper splinting techniques ensure that fractures are adequately supported until the injured individual receives comprehensive medical treatment. For detailed guidance on how to correctly apply splints, refer to paragraph 14-13, which provides specific instructions and considerations for effective splintering in a tactical environment. 252BTIER 2 SKILLS FOR THE TREATMENT OF FRACTURES 13-13. The "S" in MARCH-PAWS protocol denotes splinting, a crucial step in managing both open and closed fractures. For more information on fractures see paragraph 14-10 on page 122. Splinting involves immobilizing the injured limb to prevent further movement, typically using semi-rigid splints or improvised materials like boards or tree limbs. It's essential to incorporate the joints above and below the fracture site for stability and secure the splint firmly with wraps, belts, or tape. Additionally, securing arm fractures to the shirt using the sleeve as a sling can provide added support. However, caution must be exercised to avoid excessive tightness, which can compromise circulation to the fingers or toes. 13-14. Caution must be taken when splinting to ensure that it is not wrapped too tightly. If wrapped too tightly, the splint may cut off circulation below the splint. If there is numbness, tingling or increased pain, or if the fingers or toes turn pale or bluish, loosen the bandage. Increased swelling may occur; continued monitoring of the splintered fracture is required. 13-15. When splinting, first responders or CLS should avoid— • Manipulating the fracture site too much, resulting in pain, additional damage to blood vessels, and nerves. • Securing too tightly and cutting off blood flow. • Failing to immobilize the joint above and below the fracture when possible. • Causing further injury. • Making the casualty uncomfortable during transport or evacuation. • Splinting near or over a wound that has not been properly treated. 18BSPLINTING LEG FRACTURES 13-16. Care should be taken on cravat placement. First responders or CLS should not apply a cravat on the fracture site, as the pressure from the cravat could cause additional injury to the fracture site. 13-17. The ends of the splint should not be placed against the groin, as this could interfere with blood circulation. Extra padding is used for joints or sensitive areas, such as the groin. 13-18. Before splinting a suspected fracture, the first responder or CLS should— • Identify the location of the fracture. • Check the pulse below the fracture. • Watch for signs of poor circulation, including coolness, numbness, or lack of a pulse. • Ensure the ends of the rigid objects are not interfering with blood circulation. • If there are any signs of poor circulation, loosen the splint, reposition, and reapply. 13-19. The first responder or CLS should follow the below when applying a leg splint: • Apply the splint to the injured extremity with the limb in the position of function or a normal resting position if possible. • Secure the splint in place with appropriate materials. • Ensure the joints above and below the fracture are immobilized in the splint whenever possible. • Recheck the pulse after applying the splint. • Watch for signs of poor circulation, including coolness, numbness, or lack of a pulse. Ensure the ends of the rigid objects are not interfering with blood circulation. If there are any signs of poor circulation, loosen the splint, reposition, and reapply. • Administering the CWMP as needed. • Document all treatment on a DD Form 1380 and attach it to the casualty.

Chapter 13 124 ATP 4-02.11 23 March 2026 19BSPLINTING ARM FRACTURES 13-20. Movement or manipulation of a fractured extremity may result in increased pain. The following will help to reduce the casualty’s pain: • If possible, have the casualty support their injured arm while preparing the equipment. • Mold the padded splint using the casualty's unaffected limb to avoid unnecessary manipulation. • Use cravats or gauze bandages to immobilize the fracture and secure the limb to the body to minimize unnecessary movement during transport. 13-21. The first responder or CLS should follow the following when applying an arm splint: • Place rigid objects so that one is on each side of the injured arm or forearm. • Positioning the rigid objects so that the joint above the fracture and the joint below the fracture will be immobilized. • Apply padding between the arm and the splint. • Secure the splint with cravats, gauze bandages, strips of cloth, or other securing materials. • If possible, place two cravats above and two below the fracture site. • Use square knots to secure bandages tied away from the body on the splint. • Check pulses lower to the affected extremity before and after the application of the splint. • Administering the CWMP as needed. • Document all treatment on a DD Form 1380 and attach it to the casualty. 253BEXPEDIENT TECHNIQUES FOR SPLINTS, PADDING, BANDAGES, SLINGS, AND SWATHES 13-22. Splints may be improvised from such items such as boards, poles, sticks, tree limbs, or cardboard. If nothing is available for a splint, the chest wall can be used to immobilize a fractured arm, and the uninjured leg can be used to immobilize (to some extent) the fractured leg. 13-23. It is often impossible to be sure if a casualty has a fractured spinal column. Be suspicious of any back injury, especially if the casualty has fallen or if their back has been sharply struck or bent. If a casualty has received such an injury and does not have feeling in their legs or cannot move them, you can be reasonably sure that they have a severe back injury which is managed as a fracture. A neck fracture or injury to the back should always be suspected, and it is often impossible to be sure if a casualty has a fractured spinal column. If the spine is fractured (figure 13-28 step A on page 137), bending it can cause the sharp bone fragments to bruise or cut the spinal cord and result in permanent paralysis or death. The spinal column must maintain normal spinal position at the lower back (lumbar region) to help remove pressure from the spinal cord. 13-49. If the casualty is not to be transported until medical personnel arrive— • Caution them not to move. Ask if they are in pain or, if they are unable to move any part of their body. • Leave them in the position in which they were found. Take care not to place so much bulky padding under your casualty, as this will cause potential damage and cause undue pressure on the spine. • If the casualty is lying face down, DO NOT put anything under any part of their body.

23 March 2026 ATP 4-02.11 141 Chapter 14 Expedient Techniques for other Secondary Injuries 254BOVERVIEW OF SECONDARY INJURIES 14-1. Because medical personnel will not always be readily available, nonmedical personnel must rely on themselves and other Service members’ knowledge and fundamentals of first aid for secondary injuries until medical assistance is gained and initiated. This section will provide additional first aid, non-TCCC, procedures that nonmedical personnel can use in a garrison environment, or in combat situations. 25BABDOMINAL WOUNDS 14-2. The most serious abdominal wound is one in which an object penetrates the abdominal wall and pierces internal organs or large blood vessels. In these instances, bleeding may be severe, and death can occur rapidly. 14-3. The first step in treating an abdominal wound is to position the casualty. Place and maintain the casualty on their back with their knees in an upright (flexed) position (figure 14-1). The knees-up position helps relieve pain, assists in the treatment of shock, prevents further exposure of the bowel (intestines) or abdominal organs, and helps relieve abdominal pressure by allowing the abdominal muscles to relax. Figure 14-1. The casualty positioned (lying) on their back with their knees (flexed) up 14-4. Expose the wound by— • Removing the casualty's loose clothing to expose the wound. However, DO NOT attempt to remove clothing that is stuck to the wound; removing it may cause further injury. • Gently pick up any organs that may be on the ground. Do this with a clean, dry dressing or with the cleanest available material. Place the organs on top of the casualty's abdomen (figure 14-2). Figure 14-2. Protruding organs placed near the wound

Chapter 14 142 ATP 4-02.11 23 March 2026 Note. DO NOT probe, clean, or try to remove any foreign object from the abdomen. DO NOT touch with bare hands any exposed organs. DO NOT push organs back inside the body. 14-5. It may be necessary to wear improvised dressing (for example strips of cloth, a t-shirt, or the cleanest material available). Stabilize any protruding or impaled objects and apply a sterile abdominal dressing as follows: Note. Protruding abdominal organs should be kept moist to prevent the tissue from drying out. A moist sterile dressing should be applied if available. • Using the sterile side of the dressing, or other clean material, place any protruding organs near the wound. (DO NOT try to push organs back inside the body.) • Ensure that the dressing is large enough to cover the entire mass of protruding organs or area of the wound. • If large enough to cover the affected area, place the sterile side of the plastic wrapper directly over the wound. • Moisten the dressing with clean water prior to placing a dressing over the exposed organs. • Place the dressing directly on top of the wound or plastic wrapper, if used. • Tie the dressings loosely at the casualty’s side. 14-6. If two dressings are needed to cover a large wound, repeat steps in paragraph 15-5. If necessary, loosely cover the dressing with a cravat, elastic bandage, or gauze bandage. Tie them on the side of the casualty opposite to that of the dressing ties. 14-7. To avoid causing further injury to the casualty— • Do not touch any exposed organs. • Do not try to push any exposed organs back into the body. • Do not tie the dressing tails tightly or directly over the wound. • Do not give the casualty anything by mouth. Note. Continue to evaluate the casualty and provide necessary first aid. 14-8. Prepare the casualty for evacuation as follows: • Place the casualty on their back (face up) with the knees flexed. • Keep the patient warm, cover with a blanket as needed. • If evacuation is delayed, check the casualty for shock every five minutes. • Seek medical aid. • Record the procedures applied on DD Form 1380. 14-9. The first responder continues to evaluate the casualties and is prepared to perform basic first aid measures. Always check for both entry and exit wounds. If there are two wounds (entry and exit), treat the wound that appears more serious first (for example, the heavier bleeding, protruding organs, larger wound, and so forth). It may be necessary to improvise dressings for the second wound by using strips of cloth, a t- shirt, or the cleanest material available. 14-10. Use the casualty’s dressing from the first aid kit, not your own. If the dressing is not large enough to cover the entire wound, the plastic wrapper from the dressing may be used to cover the wound first (placing the dressing on top). Open the plastic wrapper carefully without touching the inner surface. If necessary, other improvised dressings may be made from clothing, blankets, or the cleanest materials available. 14-11. Hypothermia prevention measures are taken with abdominal injuries due to the risk of rapid heat loss from the exposed abdominal cavity or organs. Moisten the dressing with clean water prior to placing a dressing over the exposed organs and seeking medical assistance.

Expedient bandaging techniques are of paramount importance for the U.S. military due to their ability to provide immediate and effective medical care in combat situations. In the fast-paced and unpredictable nature of military operations, Service members often face severe injuries that require immediate attention to stabilize the wounded and prevent further harm. Expedient bandaging techniques enable military personnel to apply life-saving measures to control bleeding and increase the chances of survival for injured personnel. These techniques not only buy valuable time until medical help arrives but also contribute to the overall mission readiness by ensuring that Service members can continue their duties with confidence and knowing that essential medical support is readily available when needed. 123BSHOULDER BANDAGE 14-13. If an assistant is available, one person should immobilize the object while the other applies the dressings and bandages. • If necessary, apply direct pressure using gloved hands on either side of the object. • Place several layers of bulky dressings around the injury site so that the dressings surround the object. • Use additional bulky materials or dressings to build up the area around the object. • Apply the support bandages. • Apply the bandage over the bulky support material to hold it in place. • Apply the bandage tightly but not so tightly as to impair circulation or breathing. • Check circulation after applying the support bandages. Note. If a pulse was felt on an extremity and cannot be felt after the bandage has been applied, the bandage must be loosened until a pulse can be felt.

23 March 2026 ATP 4-02.11 151 Chapter 15 Casualty Monitoring and Evacuation Preparation 258BCASUALTY MONITORING 15-1. After the first responder and CLS have treated the casualty in CUF and TFC phase of TCCC they may be required to continue to monitor the casualty and prepare the casualty for evacuation. The first responder and CLS cannot treat a casualty and then forget about them. The casualty must be continually monitored and reassessed prior to the casualty’s evacuation. The continued monitoring utilizing the MARCH-PAWS sequence will allow the first responder and CLS to identify changes in the casualty’s condition and initiate those interventions necessary to prevent unnecessary death. 15-2. Casualty monitoring follows the same MARCH-PAWS process and will guide the first responder and CLS through their reassessments. After the initial casualty assessment and any treatments that are performed, the casualty must be reassessed every 15 minutes, or if seriously wounded every five to 10 minutes. The reassessment should start by reexamining any massive bleeding issues or interventions, should proceed through the rest of the MARCH-PAWS sequence, and be repeated until that casualty is transferred to the care of medical personnel. 15-3. The first responder or CLS should next evaluate any changes in respiratory status, look for signs or symptoms of shock, hypothermia, or head injuries. Also, monitor the casualty's respiratory rate, pulse, and level of consciousness. Assessing the casualty's respiratory status involves checking the rate and the quality of the respirations. By looking, listening, and feeling for breaths on the cheek, the respiratory rate can be determined (documented in the number of breaths per minute) and the respiratory effort (shallow breaths, difficulties moving air in and out, and loss of air movement on one side of the chest). 15-4. If a casualty becomes unconscious or breathing rate drops below eight respirations within one minute, insert an NPA. The casualty must be reassessed for tension pneumothorax and treated as necessary by performing an NDC. The NDC must be reassessed to confirm that it was successful. Document the rate, respiratory effort, and time assessed on DD Form 1380. If the casualty's respiratory status begins to change, reassess their status using the same approach used in the tactical trauma assessment. 15-5. The level of consciousness is best expressed by addressing the casualty's response using the AVPU method. Document any AVPU assessments or any changes in the casualty's status on the DD Form 1380. This documentation helps medical personnel better understand the casualty's situation. Note. If the casualty is not ALERT, indicating decreased mental status, the casualty should not have weapons or communications equipment. 15-6. Assessing the casualty's circulation status is done by checking for pulses. Depending on the casualty and their injuries, the first responder and CLS can check the casualty's pulse at the carotid artery (neck) or radial artery (wrist). The first responder and CLS should use their index and middle fingers, NOT their thumb, to check pulses (figure 15-1 on page 152). Document pulse rates, locations, and time taken on the DD Form 1380. Note. The absence of a radial pulse is an indication that the casualty is in shock.

When requesting MEDEVAC, several preparatory actions are crucial for ensuring the casualty's safety and stability during transport. Casualty Monitoring and Evacuation Preparation 23 March 2026 ATP 4-02.11 157 260BEVACUATION EQUIPMENT AND CASUALTY PACKAGING 15-25. Essential evacuation equipment (for example, litters, packaging materials, and BVMs) should be prepared by other unit personnel while medical treatment continues and coordinating with the casualty treatment team to save time. For example, other unit members can prepare litters while treatment is being provided. Do not delay getting casualties onto litters. The first responder and CLS can better prevent hypothermia by getting casualties off the ground. 13BLITTERS 15-26. Casualty movement in TFC may be better accomplished using litter due to the tactical situation and the need to move casualties rapidly. The litter exists only to facilitate casualty movement, and the casualty can be placed in the best position that facilitates their care and comfort. Casualties do not have to be placed on their backs on a litter. It is easier to move them if they are already on the litter; however, they must be secured to the litter before movement. Litter is also usually better for moving a casualty long distance. 15-27. All unit members should know how to open and set up litters and rehearse their use during pre-mission training. All unit members should know who will carry litter or where litter is located on vehicles. 15-28. Selecting the proper litter is dependent on several different factors: • The evacuation platform. • The terrain at the location of pick-up. • The casualty’s injuries. • The availability of different types of litters. 15-29. Two of the more common litters often used are the quad-folding litter and the lightweight flexible stretchers. Each of them has advantages and disadvantages and maybe the proper litter depends on the situation. For example, flexible litter can be moved using a one-person drag (terrain permitting) but are more difficult to carry longer distances than a quad-folding litter. 15-30. Each unit will have litters that have been proven to support their mission profile, and it is important to be aware of the limitations and advantages of each litter at your disposal before being deployed in a situation where you will require them. 134BCASUALTY PACKAGING 15-31. When preparing a casualty for evacuation, the first responder or CLS need to anticipate the environmental factors that could prevent the casualty from remaining stable. Examples include extreme noises, vibrations, high winds from propeller washing, and exposure to cold environments from either altitude or low ambient temperatures. A plan should be developed to mitigate each of those potential threats when preparing for your casualty. 15-32. All loose ends of bandages, medical equipment, and hypothermia prevention materials should be secured. The first responder or CLS should prevent dressings and other medical items from being blown around by the rotor wash or becoming entangled with other equipment. 15-33. Loose materials can catch on anything from tree limbs to body-armor of litter bearers, to parts of the aircraft or vehicles. Any snag like this can cause delays in evacuation or even further injury to casualties or providers. Blankets and foil-based hypothermia materials are especially susceptible to being caught in the wind. 15-34. Hypothermia prevention equipment should be tucked and secured beneath the casualty and litter straps. Loose edges can be caught up in wind or rotor wash or snagged on objects in the helicopter as the casualty is loaded aboard. 15-35. The TQs should remain visible and not be hidden. The DD Form 1380 should be attached to the casualty.

A spinal injury should be expected in certain situations, like fast-roping falls or being near a significant blast. In those cases, when tactically feasible, ensure the C-spine is immobilized and the casualty is kept straight during evacuation. Keep the litter type and evacuation platform in mind and ensure the evacuation ground or air vehicle can accommodate the selected litter. 372BWalking Wounded 15-37. Not all casualties require a litter for evacuation. For those casualties who are still ambulatory, provide instructions or assistance as needed. Depending on the nature of their injuries, they may be able to assist with carrying litters or providing security. 15-38. It is best to guide disoriented or visually impaired casualties by having them place their hand on the shoulder of the casualty in front of them, or a nonmedical attendant as they move to the evacuation platform. Instruct them on repeatedly checking their own wounds and dressings to ensure that bleeding remains controlled throughout the evacuation process. 261BCASUALTY STAGING 15-39. A particular importance when moving more than one casualty is the process of staging the casualties. Based on the guidance from the MEDEVAC personnel, certain casualties have priority and may need to be loaded last, so that they are the first ones offloaded at the destination. 15-40. If not given specific guidance, place the most serious casualty in a position where they are loaded last, and have casualties who may be less severely injured loaded before them. The first responder or CLS may also need to assist in marking the LZ, providing security, or assisting in marshalling the aircraft or litter- bearer teams. 262BEVACUATION CARE AFTER-ACTION REVIEW 15-41. It is critical that documentation of personnel, injury, and treatment be annotated using DD Form 1380 and should be completed prior to any handoff of the casualty. If care cannot be documented using the DD Form 1380 at the point of care by the first responder or CLS, it should be documented using the TCCC after action review, found on the JTS website, as soon as possible (within 72 hours) after treatment. 23 March 2026 ATP 4-02.11 159 291BPART THREE 294BFIRST AID PROCEDURES FOR NON-TACTICAL COMBAT CASUALTY CARE INJURIES In the operational environment, Service members are exposed to risks and receive injuries beyond those caused by an operational event. First aid skills play a vital role in ensuring the safety and well-being of Service members. As personnel participate in outdoor activities and training, the potential for accidents or injuries increases. Having a solid foundation in first aid equips Service members with the necessary knowledge and abilities to respond swiftly and effectively in times of emergencies. Whether it's treating minor cuts and bruises, providing initial care for more serious injuries, or even saving lives, the importance of first aid skills cannot be overstated. By acquiring these skills, Service members not only become more responsible and capable individuals, but they also contribute to creating a safer environment for themselves and others. Chapter 16 Bites and Stings 263BOVERVIEW OF BITES AND STINGS 16-1. Bites and stings are common occurrences that can happen in almost every environment. From pesky mosquito bites to venomous snakebites, these encounters with creatures big and small can lead to a range of discomfort, pain, and even potential danger. Understanding the various types of bites and stings, their causes, and proper treatment is crucial for minimizing the associated risks and ensuring a swift recovery. 16-2. Poison and venom are terms often used interchangeably, but they have distinct differences in their mode of delivery and the way they affect living organisms. A poison is a substance that is harmful or lethal when ingested, inhaled, or absorbed through the skin. It is typically produced by plants, animals, or microorganisms as a defensive mechanism. Poisonous substances can be found in various forms, such as toxins in certain plants, chemicals in household products, or even certain medications when taken in excessive amounts. The key characteristic of poison is that it needs to be ingested or absorbed into the body to cause harm. 16-3. Venom is a specialized secretion that is actively injected into another organism. It is typically produced by certain animals, such as snakes, spiders, scorpions, and some insects. Venom is delivered through specialized organs, such as fangs, stingers, or spines, and is primarily used for hunting or self-defense. Unlike poison, venom is actively injected into the victim's bloodstream, tissues, or body cavities, often leading to localized or systemic effects, which can range from pain and swelling to paralysis or even death. The main distinction between poison and venom lies in their delivery method. Poison is harmful when ingested or absorbed, while venom is specifically injected into another organism through specialized organs. 16-4. If bites and stings are not treated promptly and correctly, they may cause serious illness or death. The severity of a snakebite depends upon whether the snake is venomous or nonvenomous, the type of snake, the location of the bite, and the amount of venom injected. Bites from humans and other animals, such as dogs, cats, bats, raccoons, and rats, can cause severe bruises and infection and tears or lacerations of tissue. Awareness of the potential sources of injuries can reduce or prevent them from occurring. Knowledge and prompt application of first aid measures can lessen the severity of injuries from bites and stings and keep the Service member from becoming a serious casualty.

Chapter 16 160 ATP 4-02.11 23 March 2026 264BHUMAN OR ANIMAL BITES 16-5. First aid for human or animal bites aims to prevent infection and provide initial care for the wound. To perform first aid for a human or animal bite: • Remove yourself from further harm. If dealing with an animal bite, ensure that you are no longer at risk of being bitten again. • Control bleeding. If the bite wound is bleeding, apply direct pressure with a clean cloth or sterile gauze to stop or minimize the bleeding. Elevating the wound, if possible, can also help reduce bleeding. • Clean the wound. Rinse the bite wound thoroughly with clean water or saline solution to flush out any dirt, bacteria, or saliva that may have entered the wound. Gently remove any debris from the wound using mild soap and water. • Apply an antiseptic. After cleaning, apply an antiseptic solution or ointment to the wound to help reduce the risk of infection. Follow the instructions on the product label and ensure it is suitable for use on open wounds. • Cover the wound. Use a sterile dressing or clean bandage to cover the wound. This will protect it from further contamination and promote healing. Change dressing regularly to maintain cleanliness. • Seek medical attention. It is important to seek medical evaluation for all animal bites, especially those from unfamiliar or wild animals, deep wounds, or those that become red, swollen, or increasingly painful. A health care professional can assess the severity of the bite, prescribe antibiotics if necessary, and administer tetanus prophylaxis if required. 16-6. If someone gets bitten by an animal, whether known, unknown, wild, or domestic, the primary concern is rabies. Unless the animal is someone's pet and verified to be up to date on rabies, the individual who has been bitten must get the rabies post-exposure vaccine. Seemingly minor bites can lead to infection, so it is essential to consult a health care professional to determine the appropriate course of action and receive any necessary medical treatment. Note. If unable to capture or kill the animal, provide medical personnel with any information that will help identify it. 135BMARINE (SEA) ANIMALS 16-7. Except for sharks and barracuda, most marine animals will not deliberately attack. The most frequent injuries from marine animals are wounds by biting, stinging, or puncturing. Wounds inflicted by marine animals can be very painful but are rarely fatal. 16-8. Wounds from sharks, barracuda, and crocodilian can involve major trauma because of bites and lacerations. Bites from large marine animals are potentially the most life-threatening of all injuries from marine animals. Major wounds from these animals can be treated by controlling the bleeding, preventing shock, giving basic life support, splinting the injury, and by securing prompt medical aid. 16-9. Turtles, moray eels, and corals normally inflict minor wounds. Treat by cleansing the wound(s) thoroughly and by splinting if necessary. 16-10. Jellyfish, anemones, and others marine animals inflict injury by means of stinging cells in their tentacles. Contact with the tentacles produces burning pain with a rash and small hemorrhages on the skin. Shock, muscular cramping, nausea, vomiting, and respiratory distress may also occur. Gently remove the clinging tentacles with a towel and wash or treat the area. Use diluted ammonia or alcohol, a meat tenderizer, and talcum powder. If symptoms become severe or persist, seek medical assistance. 16-11. Spiny fish, urchins, stingrays, and cone shells inject their venom by puncturing the skin with their spines. General signs and symptoms include swelling, nausea, vomiting, generalized cramps, diarrhea, muscular paralysis, and shock. Deaths are rare. Treatment consists of soaking the wound(s) in hot water (when available) for 30 to 60 minutes. This inactivates the heat sensitive toxin. In addition, further first aid measures should be taken such as controlling bleeding or applying a dressing. This should be carried out as necessary.

Bites and Stings 23 March 2026 ATP 4-02.11 161 CAUTION Be careful not to scald the casualty with water that is too hot because the pain of the wound will mask the normal reaction to heat. 136BSNAKE BITES 16-12. Snakebites can occur unexpectedly during outdoor activities or encounters with snakes in their natural habitats. Understanding how to identify snakes, knowing the proper steps to take after a snakebite, and having a grasp of basic first aid techniques can significantly increase the chances of a positive outcome in such situations. Snakes are categorized between nonvenomous and venomous snakes. 16-13. Snakes can be categorized into various groups based on different characteristics. One common classification system categorizes snakes into four main categories of colubrid snakes, constrictor snakes, non- venomous snakes, and venomous snakes. These categories may overlap, and some snakes may possess traits from multiple categories. Understanding the different categories of snakes can aid in snake identification, assessing potential risks, and knowing how to respond appropriately in various situations. 373BColubrid Snakes 16-14. Colubrid snakes represent the largest snake family and include a wide range of non-venomous species. These snakes have diverse habitats, sizes, and feeding habits. Common colubrid snakes include rat, king, gopher, and water snakes. 374BConstrictor Snakes 16-15. 23 March 2026 ATP 4-02.11 173 Chapter 17 Climatic and Environmental Injuries 26BOVERVIEW OF CLIMATIC INJURIES 17-1. Climatic injuries, also known as weather-related injuries, occur when people's health is negatively affected by extreme weather conditions. These injuries can range from heat-related illnesses to cold-related conditions, and they are often a result of prolonged exposure to harsh environmental elements. Climate plays a significant role in determining the risks individuals face, with hot climates posing dangers of heat exhaustion and heatstroke, while cold climates can lead to frostbite and hypothermia. Understanding the signs, symptoms, and prevention strategies for these climatic injuries is essential in ensuring our well-being and staying safe in different weather conditions. 17-2. Specialized clothing and equipment (such as cold weather gear) for a specific environment should be obtained and used properly. For information on the prevention of heat and cold injuries, refer to TC 4-02.3, Field Hygiene and Sanitation. 17-3. Personal factors can significantly influence health and well-being in a climatic environment. Some personal factors that play a role are: • Physical Health and Fitness: A person's physical health and fitness levels affect how they cope with different climatic conditions. Individuals with good overall physical health, including cardiovascular fitness, strength, and endurance, are generally more resilient to extreme temperatures, humidity, and other climate-related challenges. • Adaptability: Personal adaptability and the ability to adjust to changing climatic conditions can impact well-being. Some people are naturally more adaptable to different climates, while others may struggle with the challenges posed by extreme temperatures, high humidity, or other climatic factors. • Sensitivity and Allergies: Some individuals may be more sensitive to specific climate-related factors, such as pollen, air pollution, or mold, which can trigger allergies or respiratory issues. Understanding personal sensitivities and taking necessary precautions can help maintain health and well-being in a climatic environment. • Mental Resilience: Mental resilience plays a vital role in dealing with challenging climatic conditions.
