Heat injury prevention is of utmost importance in the military, where Service members face intense physical challenges and operate in diverse climatic conditions. When the body gets overheated, it can lead to serious health risks and impair a Service member’s ability to perform their duties effectively. Heat-related injuries, such as heat exhaustion and heat stroke, can be prevented through various measures, including wearing appropriate clothing, taking regular rest breaks, acclimatization and fluid replacement. By prioritizing heat injury prevention, Leaders ensure the well-being and operational readiness of their personnel, allowing them to fulfill their responsibilities and accomplish their missions with strength and resilience. 17-6. Exertional heat illness refers to a spectrum of heat-related conditions that occur when the body's core temperature rises excessively during physical activity or exercise. It is primarily caused by prolonged exertion in hot and humid environments, leading to an imbalance between heat production and heat dissipation. Exertional heat illness encompasses various conditions ranging from mild heat exhaustion to severe heat stroke, which is a medical emergency. Symptoms of heat injuries may include: • Fatigue. • Dizziness. • Headache. • Nausea. • Excessive sweating. • Rapid heartbeat. • Confusion. • Loss of consciousness in severe cases. 17-7. Prompt recognition and treatment of exertional heat illness are essential to prevent complications and potentially life-threatening consequences. Effective prevention strategies, such as acclimatization, appropriate clothing, fluid replacement, and regular rest breaks, are crucial in minimizing the risk of exertional heat illness. For more information on heat illness refer to TB MED 507 and TC 4-02.3. 17-8. While there is a range of adverse effects that can result from the body overheating, the two major kinds of heat illnesses that are referred to as heat casualties are heat exhaustion (can be mild or more severe) or heat stroke. Heat stroke is the most severe form of heat illness and possibly fatal. Note. For more information on heat illness prevention, refer to the Defense Centers for Public Health – Aberdeen website. 146BHEAT EXHAUSTION 17-9. Heat exhaustion is a heat-related condition that occurs when the body becomes overheated due to prolonged exposure to high temperatures and inadequate fluid replacement. It is considered a milder form of heat illness compared to heat stroke. Signs and symptoms of heat exhaustion may include: • Heavy sweating.

Climatic and Environmental Injuries 23 March 2026 ATP 4-02.11 175 • Weaknesses and fatigue. • Dizziness or lightheadedness. • Headache. • Nausea or vomiting. • Pale, cool, or clammy skin. • Rapid and shallow breathing. • Elevated heart rate. • Muscle cramps. • Feeling faint or fainting. 17-10. If a Service member is suspected to have heat exhaustion, immediate first aid treatment should be provided. The first aid steps to treat heat exhaustion are: • Move the Service member to a cooler environment: Get them out of the heat and into a shaded or air-conditioned area. • Encourage rest and rehydration: Have the Service member lie down and elevate their legs slightly. Provide them with cool water and or an electrolyte-containing sports drink to sip on. Avoid alcohol or caffeine. • Cool the Service member's body: Loosen or remove any tight or unnecessary clothing. Apply a cool, wet cloth or towels to their skin, especially on the neck, face, and armpits. Use a fan or create air movement to aid in evaporation. • Monitor their condition: Stay with the Service member and observe their symptoms. If they do not improve within 30 minutes or their condition worsens, seek medical assistance immediately. 17-11. Heat exhaustion can progress to heat stroke, a life-threatening condition. If the person's symptoms worsen, they become disoriented, confused, or lose consciousness, immediately call for medical assistance. 17-12. Prevention is key in avoiding heat exhaustion. Practice proper fluid replacement, especially when engaging in physical activity or spending time in hot environments. Wear lightweight and loose-fitting clothing, use sunscreen, and take regular breaks in cool areas to avoid prolonged exposure to heat. 17-13. Heat exhaustion is often preceded by heat cramps, muscle cramps of the arms, legs, or abdomen. Heat cramps and heat exhaustion often act as indicators. These conditions need to be identified and treated before they get to an extreme case of heat stroke. Catch these conditions early, as the casualty needs rest, water, shade, evaluation, and possible medical care. 147BHEAT STROKE 17-14. Heat stroke is a severe and potentially life-threatening illness characterized by a rapid increase in body temperature. It occurs when the body's cooling mechanisms fail to regulate internal heat, often because of prolonged exposure to high temperatures or physical exertion in hot environments. Heat stroke is a medical emergency that requires immediate intervention. The signs and symptoms of heat stroke may include: • Altered mental state or confusion. • Headache, dizziness, or fainting. • Nausea or vomiting. • Difficulty breathing. • Hot, dry skin (lack of sweating). • High body temperature (typically above 104°Fahrenheit or 40°Celsius). • Rapid and strong heartbeat. • Seizures. 17-15. If someone is suspected of having heat stroke, it is crucial to seek emergency medical help immediately. While waiting for medical professionals to arrive, follow these first aid steps: • Move the person to a cooler location: Get them out of the heat and into a shaded or air-conditioned area as quickly as possible. • Call for emergency assistance: Dial 911 or the appropriate local emergency number to request immediate medical help to include MEDEVAC.

Chapter 17 176 ATP 4-02.11 23 March 2026 • Cool the person rapidly: Reduce their body temperature as quickly as possible. You can immerse the person in a tub of cold water, use ice cooling sheets or apply cold water to their body using wet towels or sponges. Fan the person while misting them with cool water to enhance cooling. • Monitor their vital signs: Keep a close eye on the person's breathing, pulse, and level of consciousness. If they stop breathing and you can no longer find a pulse, begin CPR if you are trained to do so. 17-16. It's important to note that heat stroke is a severe condition, and professional medical treatment is essential. Rapid cooling of the body is crucial in preventing potential organ damage and reducing the risk of complications. 17-17. To prevent heat stroke, it is important to avoid excessive physical exertion in hot environments, wear lightweight and breathable clothing, and take regular breaks in cool areas. Understanding the signs and symptoms of heat stroke and promptly seeking medical help can save lives. Note. The same person should observe the Service member during cooling and evacuation to spot symptom changes. 148BHYPONATREMIA (WATER INTOXICATION) 17-18. Hyponatremia (water intoxication) is a condition characterized by abnormally low levels of sodium in the blood. Sodium plays a crucial role in maintaining the body's fluid balance and proper nerve and muscle function. When sodium levels become significantly diluted, usually due to excessive water intake or inadequate sodium intake, hyponatremia can occur. The signs and symptoms of hyponatremia can vary depending on the severity of the condition. Common manifestations include: • Nausea and vomiting. • Headache. • Confusion or altered mental state. • Fatigue and weakness. • Seizures. • Muscle cramps or spasms. • Loss of appetite. • Swelling in the hands, feet, or legs. • Low blood pressure. • Coma (in severe cases). 17-19. If someone is suspected to have hyponatremia, it is important to seek medical attention. In the meantime, you can provide the following first aid measures: • Assess the person's condition: Check for any signs of severe symptoms such as seizures, loss of consciousness, or difficulty breathing. If any of these are present, call emergency services immediately. • Move the person to a cool, shaded area: Ensure they are away from direct sunlight or heat sources. • Encourage fluid intake: If the person is conscious and able to swallow, give them small sips of a beverage containing electrolytes, such as a sports drink. This can help restore sodium levels. • Do not give more water. Providing additional water will make the casualty more hyponatremic. • If awake, allow the Service member to consume salty foods or snacks. • Monitor the person's vital signs: Keep an eye on their breathing, heart rate, and level of consciousness. If their condition worsens, be prepared to administer CPR if necessary. 17-20. Hyponatremia can be mistaken for heat stroke, and the treatment is very different. Hyponatremia is a medical emergency that requires professional diagnosis and treatment. It is important to address the underlying cause and restore sodium levels under the guidance of a health care professional. Note. This condition most often occurs during initial entry training; however, it may occur anytime when overhydration is encountered.

Climatic and Environmental Injuries 23 March 2026 ATP 4-02.11 177 268BCOLD WEATHER INJURIES 17-21. Preventing cold weather injuries is a vital aspect of military training and operations in cold climates. When Service members face extreme cold conditions, they are at risk of various cold weather injuries, such as frostbite and hypothermia, which can significantly impact their ability to fulfill their duties effectively. Cold weather injury prevention measures are essential to ensure the well-being and operational readiness of military personnel. By implementing strategies such as proper clothing layering, maintaining adequate hydration, practicing cold weather survival techniques, and promoting awareness of cold weather risks, the military prioritizes the safety and health of its Service members. By emphasizing cold weather injury prevention, the military ensures that its personnel can endure the challenging cold environments and accomplish their missions with strength, resilience, and readiness. 17-22. Cold weather injuries encompass various conditions that occur due to exposure to extreme cold temperatures. The main cold weather injuries are: • Frostbite. • Hypothermia. • Trench Foot. • Nonfreezing injuries (such as chilblains and snow blindness). 17-23. These injuries are often caused by a combination of factors. Prolonged exposure to cold temperatures, inadequate protection against the cold, wet clothing, wind chill. Other contributing factors include poor nutrition, dehydration, fatigue, and certain medical conditions can increase the susceptibility to cold weather injuries. Proper preparation, adequate clothing, layering, regular breaks to warm up, maintain hydration, and practicing good cold weather safety measures can help reduce the risk of cold weather injuries. For more information on heat illness prevention, refer to the Defense Centers for Public Health–Aberdeen (Cold Weather Casualties and Injuries) website. For additional information on cold weather injuries refer to TC 4- 02.3. 149BFROSTBITE 17-24. Frostbite is a cold weather injury that occurs when tissues freeze due to prolonged exposure to extreme cold temperatures. It typically affects extremities, such as the fingers, toes, ears, and nose, but can also occur in other exposed areas of the body. The signs and symptoms of frostbite may vary depending on the severity, and they can include: • Cold, pale, or bluish skin. • Numbness or a loss of sensation in the affected area. • Tingling or a “pins and needles” sensation. • Hard or waxy appearance of the skin. • Swelling or blistering (in severe cases). • Pain or a burning sensation (as the affected area rewarms). • Blackened or gangrenous tissue (in severe, untreated cases). 17-25. If someone is suspected of having frostbite, it is important to provide immediate first aid and seek medical attention. Take the following first aid steps: • Move to a warm environment: Get the person out of the cold and into a warm area as soon as possible to prevent further damage. • Remove wet or constrictive clothing: Take off any wet clothing or accessories that could contribute to heat loss or restrict blood flow to the affected area. • Gradually rewarm the affected area: Immerse the frostbit area in warm (not hot) water or use warm compresses. Avoid using direct heat sources like fires or heating pads, as the person may not be able to sense heat properly and could burn the skin. • Avoid rubbing or massaging the area: Vigorous rubbing can further damage the tissues. Let the affected area rewarm naturally. • Protect and elevate the affected area: Once the frostbitten area has thawed, cover it with a sterile dressing or clean cloth. Keep the area elevated to reduce swelling, if possible.

Chapter 17 178 ATP 4-02.11 23 March 2026 • Offer pain relief if needed: Over-the-counter pain relievers like ibuprofen can help alleviate pain and reduce inflammation. However, consult a health care professional before administering any medication. • Seek medical attention: Frostbite requires medical evaluation and treatment. Even if the frostbite appears mild, professional medical care is essential to assess the extent of the injury and prevent complications. 17-26. Frostbite can cause long-term damage, including tissue loss and nerve damage. Prompt and appropriate treatment is crucial for minimizing complications and maximizing recovery. 17-27. Frostbite accounts for the largest number of cold weather injuries each year and occurs when tissue is exposed to temperatures that are usually below 32°Fahrenheit depending upon wind chill factor, length of exposure, and adequacy of protection. 17-28. Frostbite can occur suddenly due to contact with cold metal or super-cooled liquids such as alcohol, fuel, or antifreeze or can develop over time due to prolonged cold exposure. Frostbite is most common in exposed skin such as the nose, ears, cheeks, but can also occur in the hands and feet due to reduced blood flow. Note. The onset is signaled by a sudden blanching of the skin of the nose, ears, cheeks, fingers, or toes followed by a momentary tingling sensation. Frostbite is indicated when the face, hands, or feet stop hurting. 150BHYPOTHERMIA 17-29. Hypothermia is a concern regarding TCCC and the body’s ability to form clots is impaired. This condition can cause a tendency toward prolonged or excessive bleeding, which may occur spontaneously or following an injury. Hypothermia is a potentially life-threatening condition that occurs when the body's core temperature drops significantly below normal. 17-30. The risks differ with environmental hypothermia. Victims of moderate to severe environmental hypothermia are known to have a risk of an irregular heartbeat associated with “afterdrop.” Afterdrop is the continued fall of deep body temperatures during rewarming after hypothermia. Afterdrop is thought to endanger the heart by further cooling from cold blood presumed to be returning to the body’s center or core. 17-31. Environmental hypothermic casualties should be monitored and gently handled as afterdrop is not always observed. The goals for overall casualty treatment (such as hemorrhage control and resuscitation in TCCC versus warming measures along with gentle handling in environmental hypothermia) should be understood, trained, and rehearsed. For further discussion on hypothermia see Chapter 8. 151BTRENCH FOOT 17-32. Trench foot, also known as immersion foot, is a non-freezing cold injury that occurs when the feet are exposed to prolonged damp and cold conditions. It can lead to tissue damage and infection. Contributing factors include wet and cold environments, inadequate foot hygiene, prolonged periods of immobility, and improper footwear. 17-33. Trench foot is often associated with Soldiers during World War I who endured long periods in wet trenches. Trench foot can occur in any situation where the feet are exposed to excessive moisture and cold temperatures. The signs and symptoms of trench foot include: • Redness and swelling of the feet. • Numbness or tingling sensation. • Itching or a burning sensation. • Pain or discomfort. • Blisters or open sores. • Coldness and paleness of the skin. • Foul odor. 17-34. If someone is suspected to have trench feet, the following first aid steps can be taken:

Climatic and Environmental Injuries 23 March 2026 ATP 4-02.11 179 • Move them to a warm and dry environment: Get the person out of wet and cold conditions as soon as possible to prevent further damage. • Remove wet footwear and socks: Take off wet footwear and socks to allow the feet to dry. Avoid rubbing or massaging the feet, as it can further damage the skin. • Elevate the feet: Raise the feet slightly to help reduce swelling and improve circulation. • Clean and dry the feet: Gently wash the feet with warm water (not hot) and mild soap. Pat the feet dry with a clean towel, avoiding excessive friction. • Apply clean, dry socks: Once the feet are dry, put on clean, dry socks to help insulate and protect the feet. Avoid using tight or constrictive socks. • Avoid direct heat sources: Do not use direct heat sources like fires, heaters, or heating pads to warm the feet. The affected feet may be numb, and exposure to high heat can cause burns. • Seek medical attention: It is important to seek medical evaluation and treatment for trench feet. Health care professionals can provide appropriate care, clean, and dress any blisters or open sores, and monitor any signs of infection. 17-35. Prevention is key in avoiding trench feet. Keep the feet dry, wear appropriate footwear that is waterproof and well-insulated, change wet socks and shoes promptly, and take breaks to allow the feet to dry and warm up. Proper foot hygiene and regular inspection of the feet can help identify any early signs of trench foot and prevent its progression. 152BNONFREEZING INJURIES 17-36. Exposure to temperatures from 32°Fahrenheit to 60°Fahrenheit may cause nonfreezing cold injuries of skin, fingers, toes, ears, and facial parts. Exposure of skin to cold metal; super cold fuel, petroleum, oil, and lubricants; wind chill; and the wear of tight, circulation-restricting clothing (particularly boots). 17-37. Riding in open vehicles, exposure to propeller or rotor-generated wind, running or skiing, and altitude exposure where there is little tree cover can all contribute to greater wind chill. 17-38. Nonfreezing cold injuries are chilblain and snow blindness. Trench foot occurs when tissues are exposed to temperatures from 32°Fahrenheit to 60°Fahrenheit for prolonged periods of time (>12 hours), whereas chilblains, which is a more superficial injury, can occur after repeated prolonged exposure of bare skin to low temperatures from 60°Fahrenheit down to 32°Fahrenheit. Snow blindness is caused by unprotected exposure to UV rays. Snow blindness can be prevented using appropriate eye protection (sunglasses). Snow blindness can be painful as it gets closer to three to five hours later. 37BChilblains 17-39. Chilblains, also known as pernio, is a nonfreezing cold weather injury that can occur after one to five hours in cold, wet conditions at temperatures from about 50°Fahrenheit down to 32°Fahrenheit. Chilblains are a localized inflammatory response of the skin that occurs due to prolonged exposure to cold and damp conditions. 17-40. The most affected areas are the fingernail-side of the fingers, but the ears, face, and other exposed skin are also areas of occurrence. There are no lasting effects from chilblain. They are more common in colder climates and during the winter season. The signs and symptoms of chilblains include: • Redness and inflammation of the affected area. • Itching or a burning sensation. • Swelling and tenderness. • Skin discoloration (bluish or purplish appearance). • Formation of small, fluid-filled blisters. • Dry or cracked skin. • Pain or discomfort, especially when exposed to warmth after being cold. 17-41. If someone is experiencing chilblains, the following first aid procedures can be performed: • Move to a warm environment: Get the person indoors or to a warmer area to prevent further exposure to cold temperatures.

Chapter 17 180 ATP 4-02.11 23 March 2026 • Gradually rewarm the affected areas: Avoid sudden temperature changes or direct heat sources like heaters or fires, as this can worsen the condition. Instead, gently warm the affected areas by placing them near warm body parts (such as under the armpits) or by using warm water. The water should be comfortably warm, not hot. • Protect and cover the affected areas: Once the affected areas have been warmed, keep them protected from further exposure to cold. Cover them with warm clothing, gloves, or socks to help insulate and maintain a stable temperature. • Avoid scratching or rubbing the affected areas: Itching can be intense, but scratching or rubbing can further damage the skin and increase the risk of infection. Encourage the person to resist the urge to scratch. • Apply soothing lotions or creams: If recommended by a health care professional, apply mild lotions or creams to alleviate itching and provide relief. Avoid using excessive amounts or substances that may irritate the skin. • Seek medical advice if needed: If symptoms worsen, if blisters or open sores develop, or if signs of infection (such as increased redness, swelling, or discharge) are present, it is important to seek medical attention for proper evaluation and treatment. 17-42. Preventing chilblains is essential. It can be achieved by keeping the extremities warm and dry, wearing appropriate protective clothing and footwear, avoiding prolonged exposure to cold and damp environments, and gradually acclimating the body to temperature changes. Regularly checking the skin for any signs of chilblains can help identify and address the condition early on. 378BSnow Blindness 17-43. Snow blindness, also known as photokeratitis or UV keratitis, is a condition that occurs when the eyes are exposed to excessive UV radiation, typically from sunlight reflected off snow or ice. It can also happen when exposed to other intense light sources, such as welding arcs or tanning beds. Snow blindness is essentially a temporary sunburn of the cornea, the clear front surface of the eye. The signs and symptoms of snow blindness include: • Eye pain or a sensation of grittiness. • Redness and inflammation of the eyes. • Watery eyes and excessive tearing. • Blurred vision or sensitivity to light. • Feeling as if there is something in the eye. • Headache. • Temporary vision loss in severe cases. 17-44. If someone is experiencing snow blindness, the following first aid treatment can be administered: • Move to a dark and sheltered area: Get the person indoors or to a shaded area to protect the eyes from further exposure to bright light. • Rest the eyes: Keep the eyes closed or minimize eye movements to reduce discomfort and prevent further irritation. • Avoid rubbing the eyes: Rubbing the eyes can exacerbate the condition and potentially cause additional damage. • Apply cold compresses: Place a cold, damp cloth or cool pack over closed eyes to help reduce inflammation and alleviate pain. Avoid using ice directly on the skin. • Use artificial tears: Over-the-counter artificial tear drops can be used to provide relief and moisture to the eyes. Follow the instructions on the packaging or consult a health care professional for appropriate usage. • Wear protective eyewear: If the person needs to be in a bright environment, ensure they wear sunglasses that offer 100 percent UV protection. Wrap-around sunglasses or goggles with side shields provide the best protection. • Seek medical attention: It is advisable to seek medical advice if the symptoms persist, worsen, or if vision loss occurs. A health care professional can examine the eyes and provide appropriate treatment and guidance.

Climatic and Environmental Injuries 23 March 2026 ATP 4-02.11 181 17-45. Prevention is crucial in avoiding snow blindness. To protect the eyes from excessive UV radiation, wear sunglasses or goggles that provide 100 percent UV protection, especially in snowy or high-altitude environments. Additionally, using wide-brimmed hats or visors can help shield the eyes from indirect sunlight. 269BMOUNTAINOUS TERRAIN INJURIES 17-46. Approximately 27 percent of the earth’s land surface is considered mountainous terrain. These areas are characterized by rugged landscapes, elevated peaks, and varying degrees of slope. Mountains play a crucial role in shaping the Earth’s geography, influencing climate patterns, and providing habitat for diverse ecosystems. 17-47. Service members operating in mountainous terrain should be well-prepared, have the necessary skills, and carry a first aid kit to address potential injuries and emergencies. Additionally, understanding the terrain, weather conditions, and having proper equipment can contribute to safer operations in mountainous terrain. 17-48. Mountainous terrain poses various challenges and risks, and injuries can range from minor to severe. Common injuries in mountainous terrain include: • Sprains and Strains. Uneven and rocky surfaces can lead to twisted ankles or muscle strains. • Fractures. Falls or accidents may result in broken bones, particularly in extremities. • Cuts and Abrasions. Sharp rocks and uneven surfaces can cause cuts and scrapes. • Altitude Sickness. At higher elevations, individuals may experience symptoms like headache, nausea, and dizziness due to reduced oxygen levels. • Hypothermia. Cold temperatures, especially at higher altitudes, can lead to a drop in body temperature. • Dehydration. Strenuous activity, combined with lower humidity and potential difficulty accessing water sources, can lead to dehydration. • Exhaustion. Hiking or climbing in mountainous terrain can be physically demanding, leading to fatigue and exhaustion. • Frostbite. Exposure to cold conditions, especially at high altitudes, can result in frostbite, where skin and tissues freeze. • Avalanche and Rockfall Injuries. In certain mountainous regions, avalanches or rockfalls can pose significant dangers, causing trauma and injuries. • Wildlife Encounters. Depending on the location, encounters with wildlife can lead to injuries. 17-49. Many of the above injury types and treatments have been discussed throughout this publication, however operating in mountainous terrain can be challenging, but it's crucial to be aware of the potential risks, including altered mental status, high-altitude pulmonary edema (HAPE), and high-altitude cerebral edema (HACE). 153BALTITUDE EMERGENCIES 17-50. Changes in consciousness, confusion, or disorientation can occur due to factors like altitude sickness, dehydration, or exhaustion. Recognizing and responding to an altered mental status promptly is essential for ensuring the well-being of Service members. Some general first aid measures for Service members experiencing altered mental status in mountainous terrain include: • Move to Lower Altitude: If the altered mental status is due to altitude sickness, move the Service member to a lower altitude immediately. Descending to lower elevations allows the body to acclimatize and receive more oxygen, potentially alleviating symptoms. • Rest and Hydration: Ensure the Service member rests and stays hydrated. Dehydration and fatigue can contribute to an altered mental status, so providing water and allowing for adequate rest are important. • Monitor Breathing: Keep a close eye on the Service member's breathing. Shallow or irregular breathing may indicate respiratory distress. If breathing difficulties persist, promptly seek medical assistance. • Check for Signs of Hypoxia: Assess for signs of hypoxia, which occurs when the body doesn't receive enough oxygen. Look for bluish discoloration of the lips or fingertips. If observed, it may indicate a more severe oxygen deficiency, requiring immediate medical attention.

Chapter 17 182 ATP 4-02.11 23 March 2026 • Keep Warm: If the altered mental status is due to cold temperatures, provide warmth by using blankets, jackets, or other insulating materials. Preventing hypothermia is crucial. • Monitor for Improvement or Worsening: Keep a close watch on the Service members’ condition. If there is no improvement or if the symptoms worsen, seek medical assistance as soon as possible. • Administer Oxygen (if available): If you have access to supplemental oxygen and the person is experiencing severe symptoms, administering oxygen can be beneficial. However, this may require specific training and equipment. • Evacuation if Necessary: In severe cases or if the person's condition doesn't improve, consider evacuating them to a medical facility at a lower altitude. This may involve calling for professional rescue or using available means of transportation. 17-51. First aid of an altered mental status is a temporary measure, and medical assistance should be sought for any significant or worsening symptoms. If in doubt or if the altered mental status persists, it is essential to prioritize the Service member's safety and seek timely medical help. 154BHIGH-ALTITUDE PULMONARY EDEMA 17-52. High-Altitude Pulmonary Edema is a serious condition that can occur at higher elevations, typically above 2,500 meters (8,200 feet). It involves the accumulation of fluid fluids in the lungs and can be life- threatening. Some general first aid measures for Service members experiencing HAPE in mountainous terrain include: • Immediate Descent. The most critical first aid measure for HAPE is an immediate descent to lower altitudes. Every effort should be made to get the affected individual to a lower elevation as quickly as possible, as this is the most effective way to alleviate symptoms. • Rest and Oxygen. Ensure the person rests and provide supplemental oxygen if available. Oxygen therapy can help improve oxygen levels in the blood and alleviate breathing difficulties. • Keep Warm. Maintain the person's warmth by using blankets and insulating layers. Cold temperatures can exacerbate symptoms, so preventing hypothermia is important. • Stay Hydrated. Encourage the individual to drink fluids to stay hydrated. Dehydration can worsen the condition, so maintaining adequate fluid intake is essential. • Monitor Breathing. Keep a close watch on the person's breathing. If there are signs of severe respiratory distress, such as blue lips or fingertips, it may indicate a critical situation, and professional medical help should be sought immediately. • Administer Medications (if available). In some cases, medications such as nifedipine or sildenafil may be used to help manage HAPE symptoms. The medical professional should determine the availability and use of these medications. • Evacuation. Seek evacuation to the MTF at a lower altitude as soon as possible. Evacuation may involve contacting medical personnel and requesting evacuation to a lower elevation where more definitive medical care can be provided. 17-53. HAPE is a medical emergency, and prompt action is crucial. While these first aid measures can provide initial assistance, professional medical help should be sought without delay. If you suspect someone has HAPE, it's essential to prioritize their safety and act swiftly to get them to a lower altitude and seek immediate medical attention. 15BHIGH-ALTITUDE CEREBRAL EDEMA 17-54. High-Altitude Cerebral Edema is a severe and life-threatening condition that can occur at high elevations, typically above 3,000 meters (9,800 feet). It involves swelling of the brain and can lead to neurological symptoms. Some general first aid measures for Service members experiencing HACE in mountainous terrain include: • Immediate Descent. The most critical first aid measure for HACE is an immediate and rapid descent to lower altitudes. Descending to a lower elevation is essential to reduce the impact of high altitude on the brain. • Rest and Oxygen. Ensure the affected person rests and provide supplemental oxygen if available. Oxygen therapy can help improve oxygen levels in the blood and alleviate neurological symptoms.

Climatic and Environmental Injuries 23 March 2026 ATP 4-02.11 183 • Keep Warm. Maintain the person's warmth using blankets and insulating layers. Cold temperatures can worsen symptoms, so preventing hypothermia is important. • Hydration. Encourage the individual to drink fluids to stay hydrated. Dehydration can exacerbate the condition, so maintaining adequate fluid intake is crucial. • Administer Medications (if available). In some cases, medications such as dexamethasone may be used to help manage HACE symptoms. Medical professionals should determine the use of medications, and access to such medications may be limited in remote mountainous areas. • Monitor Neurological Symptoms. Keep a close watch on the person's neurological symptoms. Signs of severe neurological impairment, such as confusion, loss of coordination, or changes in consciousness, require urgent medical attention. • Evacuation. Seek evacuation to an MTF at a lower altitude as quickly as possible. HACE is a medical emergency, and professional medical help should be sought without delay. • Reassure and calm. Keep the affected individual calm and reassure them. Stress and anxiety can exacerbate symptoms, so a supportive and calming environment is beneficial. 17-55. HACE is a critical condition, and time is of the essence. While these first aid measures can provide initial assistance, medical assistance should be sought urgently. If HACE is suspected in a Service member, prioritize their safety by facilitating a rapid descent and seeking immediate medical attention.

23 March 2026 ATP 4-02.11 185 Chapter 18 Sickle Cell Trait 270BOVERVIEW OF SICKLE CELL TRAIT 18-1. Sickle cell trait (SCT) is an inherited genetic condition in which a person carries one copy of the sickle cell gene and one normal hemoglobin gene. It is different from sickle cell disease (SCD), which occurs when a person inherits two copies of the sickle cell gene. The SCT is usually asymptomatic and generally does not cause health problems. However, under certain conditions, such as extreme physical exertion, high altitudes, or dehydration, individuals with SCT may experience complications. 18-2. SCD is a genetic disorder that affects the red blood cells, which are responsible for carrying oxygen throughout the body. It is caused by a mutation in the gene responsible for producing hemoglobin, a protein that enables red blood cells to carry oxygen. In individuals with SCD, the hemoglobin gene mutation leads to the production of abnormal hemoglobin, known as hemoglobin S. This abnormal hemoglobin causes red blood cells to become rigid and take on a sickle or crescent shape instead of their normal disc shape. These sickle-shaped cells can get stuck in small blood vessels, leading to various complications. 18-3. For more information on SCT and SCD, refer to the National Institute of Health website. Service members with SCT can typically participate fully in any physical activity. Under certain circumstances Service members with SCT may suffer negative effects such as muscle weakness, pain, and collapse. This collapse is termed exercise collapse associated with sickle cell trait (ECAST). 18-4. ECAST refers to a specific syndrome that can occur in individuals with SCT during or immediately after strenuous exercise. It is characterized by symptoms such as dizziness, weakness, fatigue, and in rare cases, collapse, or loss of consciousness. The ECAST can occur due to a mismatch between oxygen supply and demand in the muscles during intense physical activity. 18-5. The ECAST is a relatively rare occurrence, and most individuals with SCT can engage in regular physical activities without any issues. However, to minimize the risk of complications, individuals with SCT are advised to take precautions during exercise, such as staying well-hydrated, avoiding excessive heat or cold exposure, and gradually increasing the intensity and duration of physical activity. It is also recommended to consult with a health care professional for personalized guidance and address any concerns related to exercise. 18-6. The ECAST, as a cause of collapse in Service members, is considered because the relative risk of death is significantly higher in-Service members with SCT than those without. Early recognition and proper treatment of ECAST can increase survival and decrease complications. For more information on ECAST, refer to the American Medical Society for Sports Medicine website. 156BRISK FACTORS 18-7. While the exact causes of ECAST are not fully understood, there are several risk factors that can contribute to its occurrence. These include: • Strenuous exercise: Engaging in high-intensity or prolonged physical activity can increase the risk of ECAST. • Dehydration: Inadequate fluid intake or excessive fluid loss through sweating can contribute to the risk of ECAST. • Heat and humidity: Exercising in hot and humid environments can further exacerbate the risk of ECAST. 18-8. Preexisting medical conditions and environmental factors that may increase the likelihood of an ECAST episode include: • Poor Hydration. • Exercise-induced asthma. • Dietary supplements contain stimulants. • Excessive heat exposure.

Chemical agents are classified based on their properties, effects, and intended use. There are different classification systems depending on the context, such as their use in warfare, industry, or transportation. One widely used classification system for chemical agents is based on their potential harm to human health and the environment. Common chemical agent categories are: • Adversary use: Persistent agents intended to cause casualties for more than 24 hours or restrict terrain. Nonpersistent agents that can lose their ability to cause casualties after 10-15 minutes. • Hazard classification: Explosiveness (Class 1), flammability (Classes 3,4), toxicity (Class 6). • Physiological action: Nerve, blood, blister, choking, and incapacitating. • Physical state: solid, liquid, or vapor. 19-7. Different regulatory bodies and organizations may have their own specific classification systems and criteria for chemical agents, depending on the context and intended use. These classifications help in

Chapter 19 190 ATP 4-02.11 23 March 2026 identifying and managing potential hazards, ensuring appropriate handling, storage, transportation, and emergency response measures are in place. 19-8. Biological agents, also known as bioagents or biological hazards, are classified based on their potential to cause harm to living organisms, including humans. They can be categorized in various ways, considering factors such as their origin, mode of transmission, pathogenicity, and potential for use as weapons. Common classification systems for biological agents are: • Risk Group Classification: Biological agents can be classified into different risk groups based on their level of pathogenicity and the risk they pose to human health. This classification system is commonly used in research laboratories and health care settings. The risk groups range from Risk Group 1 (low individual and community risk) to Risk Group 4 (high individual and community risk). The classification is determined by considering factors such as infectivity, severity of disease, available preventive measures, and efficacy of treatment. • Biosafety Level Classification: This classification system is primarily used in laboratory settings to ensure appropriate containment measures and safety protocols are followed when handling biological agents. It categorizes agents into different biosafety levels based on their risk to laboratory personnel and the environment. The biosafety levels range from biosafety levels 1 (lowest level of risk) to biosafety levels 4 (highest level of risk). The classification is determined by factors such as pathogenicity, ease of transmission, and availability of effective preventive measures and treatments. • The U.S. Centers for Disease Control (also known as CDC) and Prevention Category A, B, and C Classification: Developed by the Centers for Disease Control, is focused on potential bioterrorism agents. Biological agents are classified into three categories: ▪ Category A: Agents that pose the highest risk to national security and public health. They have the potential for widespread dissemination, high mortality rates, and significant public panic. Examples include anthrax, smallpox, and Ebola virus. ▪ Category B: Agents that are moderately easy to disseminate and cause moderate morbidity and low mortality rates. Examples include Q fever, Brucellosis, and ricin toxin. ▪ Category C: Agents that have the potential for emerging threats and can be engineered for mass dissemination. Examples include Nipah virus, hantavirus, and emerging strains of influenza. 19-9. These classification systems help in identifying and managing biological hazards, implementing appropriate biosafety and biosecurity measures, developing effective response plans, and conducting research and surveillance activities. They are essential tools in ensuring the safe handling, containment, and prevention of the spread of biological agents. The classification of biological warfare (also known as BW) agents can vary slightly depending on the organization or country using the classification system. These classifications help guide efforts in preparedness, response planning, research, surveillance, and the development of countermeasures against potential biological warfare threats. Blister agents (vesicants) include mustard, nitrogen mustards, lewisite, and other arsenicals, mixtures of mustards and arsenicals, and phosgene oxime. Blister agents may act on the eyes, mucous membranes, lungs, and skin. They burn and blister the skin or any other body parts they contact. Even relatively low doses may cause serious injury. Blister agents damage the respiratory tract (nose, sinuses, and windpipe) when inhaled and cause vomiting and diarrhea when absorbed. Lewisite and phosgene oxime cause immediate pain on contact. However, mustard agents are deceptive as there is little or no pain at the time of exposure. In some cases, signs of injury may not appear for several hours after exposure.

First Aid in a Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear Environment 23 March 2026 ATP 4-02.11 203 385BProtective Measures for Blister Agent Poisoning 19-53. Your protective mask with hood and protective over garment provides protection against blister agents. CAUTION Large drops of liquid vesicants on the protective over garment ensemble may penetrate it if allowed to stand for an extended period. Remove large drops as soon as possible. 386BSigns and Symptoms of Blister Agent Poisoning 19-54. Immediate and intense pain upon contact with L, LH (lewisite and mustard) mixture, and phosgene oxime. No initial pain upon contact with mustard. 19-55. Inflammation and blisters (burns) resulting in tissue destruction. The severity of a chemical burn is directly related to the concentration of the agent and the duration of contact with the skin. The longer the agent is in contact with the tissue, the more serious the injury will be. 19-56. Vomiting and diarrhea. Exposure to high concentrations of vesicants may cause vomiting or diarrhea. 19-57. The blister agent vapors absorbed during ordinary field exposure will probably not cause enough internal body (systemic) damage to result in death. However, death may occur from prolonged exposure to high concentrations of vapor or from extensive liquid contamination over wide areas of the skin, particularly when decontamination is neglected or delayed. 387BFirst Aid Measures for Blister Agent Poisoning 19-58. Use your RSDL to decontaminate your skin and use water to flush contaminated eyes. Decontamination of vesicants must be done immediately (within one minute is best). 19-59. If blisters form, cover them loosely with a field dressing and secure the dressing. CAUTION Blisters are burns. DO NOT attempt to decontaminate the skin where blisters have formed, as the agent has already been absorbed. 19-60. If you receive blisters over a wide area of the body, you are considered seriously burned. Seek medical assistance immediately. 19-61. If vomiting occurs, the mask should be lifted momentarily and drained. Make sure, while doing this, the eyes are closed, and the breath is held. As soon as it is complete, replace, clear, and seal the mask. 19-62. Remember, if vomiting or diarrhea occurs after having been exposed to blister agents, seek medical assistance immediately. 168BCHOKING AGENTS (LUNG-DAMAGING AGENTS) 19-63. Chemical agents that attack lung tissue, primarily causing fluid buildup (pulmonary edema), are classified as choking agents (lung-damaging agents). This group includes phosgene, diphosgene (known as DP), chlorine (known as Cl), and chloropicrin (known as PS). Of these four agents, phosgene is the most dangerous and is more likely to be employed by the enemy in future conflict. Your protective mask gives adequate protection against choking agents.

During and immediately after exposure to choking agents (depending on agent concentration and length of exposure), you may experience some or all the following signs and symptoms: • Tears (lacrimation). • Coughing. • Choking. • Tightness of chest. • Nausea and vomiting. • Headaches. 389BSelf-Aid for Choking Agents 19-65. The protective mask should be put on immediately when any of the conditions described above exist. Another indication of a phosgene attack is an odor like newly mown hay; however, DO NOT rely upon odor as indication of a chemical attack. 19-66. If some phosgene is inhaled, normal combat duties should be continued unless there is difficulty in breathing, nausea, vomiting, or more than the usual shortness of breath during exertion. With ordinary field exposure to choking agents, death will probably not occur. Hydrogen cyanide. During any chemical attack, if you get a sudden stimulation to breathe or detect an odor like bitter almonds, PUT ON YOUR MASK IMMEDIATELY. Put your mask on immediately if you experience any irritation of the eyes, nose, or throat. The nearest Service member should mask Service members who are unable to mask themselves. If exposure to blood agents is suspected, immediate medical assistance is needed. An incapacitating agent is a chemical agent that produces temporary, disabling conditions, which persist for hours to days after exposure. Unlike riot control agents, which usually are momentary or fleeting in action, incapacitating agents have a persistent effect. It is likely that smoke-producing munitions or aerosols will disseminate such agents, thus making breathing their means of entry into the body. The protective mask is, therefore, essential. 19-75. There are no specific first aid measures to relieve the symptoms of incapacitating agents. Supportive first aid and physical restraint may be indicated. If the casualty is stuporous or comatose, be sure that respiration is unobstructed; then turn them on their side in case vomiting should occur. Complete cleansing of the skin with soap and water, this should be done as soon as possible; or RSDL can be used if washing is impossible. Remove weapons and other potentially harmful items from Service members who are suspected of having these symptoms. Harmful items include cigarettes, matches, medications, and small items that might be swallowed accidentally. Delirious (confused) persons have been known to attempt to eat items bearing only a superficial resemblance to food. 19-76. Incapacitating agents (anticholinergic drugs BZ type) may produce alarming dryness and coating of the lips and tongue; however, there is usually no danger of immediate dehydration. Fluids should be given sparingly, if at all, because of the danger of vomiting and because of the likelihood of temporary urinary retention due to paralysis of bladder muscles. 19-77. Immediate and vigorous cooling of the casualties is indicated if the body temperature is elevated and mucous membranes are dry, (as for heatstroke). The casualty can be cooled by spraying them with cool water and fanning; applying alcohol-soaked cloths and air circulation; and providing maximum exposure to air in a shaded area, along with maximum air circulation. Such cases are usually a result of anticholinergic poisoning. CAUTION DO NOT use ice for cooling the skin. 19-78. Rapid evacuation should be accomplished since medical treatment with the appropriate medication may be lifesaving. Reassurance and a firm, but friendly, attitude by individuals providing first aid will be beneficial if the casualty appears to comprehend what is being said. Conversation is a waste of time if the Service member is incoherent or cannot understand what is being said. In such cases, the less said, the better it is. These casualties will benefit more from prompt and vigorous restraint and evacuation to an MTF.

Chapter 19 206 ATP 4-02.11 23 March 2026 170BINCENDIARIES 19-79. Incendiaries can be grouped as white phosphorus (WP), thickened gasoline, metal, and oil and metal. You must learn to protect yourself against these incendiaries. 396BWhite Phosphorus 19-80. WP is primarily used as a smoke-producing agent but also serves an incendiary role for igniting field expedients and combustible materials. The burns caused by WP are typically multiple, deep, and vary in size. Once WP particles contact the skin or clothing, they will continue to burn until deprived of air, and they tend to adhere to any surface they contact, requiring physical removal. 19-81. In the event that WP particles ignite clothing, it's crucial to remove the contaminated clothing quickly to prevent the WP from burning through to the skin. If WP particles directly strike the skin, the immediate response should be to smother the flames using water, a wet cloth, or mud. It is important to note that since WP is soluble in oil, one should not use grease or oily substances to extinguish the flames as these can exacerbate the burning. 19-82. To prevent further combustion, keep the WP particles covered with wet material to exclude air. Removal of WP particles from the skin should be done cautiously using a wet cloth to brush them away and a knife, bayonet, stick, or other available tools to pick them out. 19-83. Once immediate first aid measures are taken, it is vital to seek medical assistance as soon as the mission allows us to address any burns or injuries caused by WP exposure properly. 397BThickened Fuel Mixtures (Napalm) 19-84. Thickened fuel mixtures (napalm) tend to cling to clothing and body surfaces, thereby producing prolonged exposure and severe burns. The first aid for these burns is the same as for other heat burns. The heat and irritating gases given off by these combustible mixtures may cause lung damage, which must be treated by medical personnel. 398BMetal Incendiaries 19-85. Metal incendiaries pose special problems. Thermite particles on the skin should be immediately cooled with water and then removed. The first aid for these burns is the same as for other heat burns. Particles of magnesium on the skin burn quickly and deeply. Like other metal incendiaries, they must be removed. Ordinarily, medical personnel should do the complete removal of these particles as soon as possible. Immediate medical treatment is required. 39BOil and Metal Incendiaries 19-86. Oil and metal incendiaries, upon contact with skin and clothing, produce effects similar to those caused by white phosphorus. These substances can cause severe burns that require immediate and proper first aid attention to prevent further damage and promote healing. For detailed guidance on administering first aid for burns resulting from exposure to incendiaries like oil and metal, see Chapter 12. This chapter provides comprehensive instructions on the steps to take in treating burns, including how to manage the injury before professional medical help is available. 274BFIRST AID IN A BIOLOGICAL ENVIRONMENT 19-87. Biological hazards can provide important advantages to adversaries who use them because of factors such as— • Clandestine employment. • Delayed onset of symptoms. • Detection, identification, and verification difficulties. • Agent persistence. • Communicability.

First Aid in a Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear Environment 23 March 2026 ATP 4-02.11 207 19-88. Biological attacks can result in combat ineffectiveness by introducing disease-causing organisms such as bacteria or viruses into the force through aerosol release; food and water contamination; vectors such as ticks, fleas, mosquitoes, or body fluids from infected animals or humans. The occurrence of the signs and symptoms from a biological hazard may appear in a few minutes to several hours or days to weeks depending on the biological hazard, the Service member’s susceptibility, and the amount of biological hazard that is inhaled, ingested, or deposited on the skin. Many biological warfare agents present the same signs and symptoms as the flu or common cold such as fever, cough, runny nose, and tiredness. 19-89. For certain biological warfare hazards, Service members may be directed to take doxycycline or ciprofloxacin from the initial issue medical CBRN defense materiel. 171BTOXINS 19-90. Toxins have reportedly been used in past conflicts. Witnesses and survivors have described the employment of the T-2 mycotoxin as toxic rain (or yellow rain) because it was reported to have been released from aircraft as a yellow powder or liquid that covered ground, structures, vegetation, and people. 40BSigns and Symptoms of Toxin Poisoning 19-91. The occurrence of the symptoms from toxins may appear in a period of a few minutes to several hours depending on the toxin, the Service member’s susceptibility, and the amount of toxin that is inhaled, ingested, or deposited on the skin. Symptoms from toxins usually involve the central nervous system but are often preceded by less prominent symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, cramps, stomach irritation, and burning sensation. Typical neurological symptoms often develop rapidly in severe cases; for example, visual disturbances, inability to swallow, speech difficulty, lack of muscle coordination, and sensory abnormalities (numbness of the mouth, throat, or extremities). Yellow rain (mycotoxins) also may have hemorrhagic symptoms, which could include any or all of the following: • Dizziness. • Severe itching or tingling of the skin. • Formation of multiple, small, or hard blisters. • Coughing up blood. • Shock (which could result in death). 401BSelf-Aid of Toxin Poisoning 19-92. Upon recognition of an attack employing toxins, you must immediately take the following actions: • Stop breathing, put on your protective mask with hood, and then resume breathing. Next, put on your protective ensemble. • Should itching of the face become severe or unbearable, quickly— ▪ Loosen the cap in your canteen or valve on your water source. ▪ Take and hold a deep breath and lift your mask. ▪ While holding your breath, close your eyes and flush your face with generous amounts of water. CAUTION DO NOT rub or scratch your eyes. Try not to let the water run onto your clothing or protective over garment. ▪ Put your protective mask back on, seat it properly, clear it, and check it for a seal; then resume breathing. ▪ Decontaminate your skin by bathing with soap and water as soon as the mission permits. ▪ Change clothing and decontaminate your protective mask using soap and water. Replace the filters if directed.

The mask is then replaced, cleared, and sealed. 402BMedical Assistance for Toxin Poisoning 19-94. 23 March 2026 ATP 4-02.11 209 Chapter 20 Combat and Operational Stress Control 276BOVERVIEW OF COMBAT AND OPERATIONAL STRESS CONTROL 20-1. Psychological first aid is just as crucial as physical first aid and is a familiar concept to many. Think back to when a simple comforting gesture from a parent soothed you as a child, or how supportive conversation with a friend helped you navigate through disappointment or grief. These actions are natural responses to emotional distress, similar to how we instinctively want to help someone who is physically hurt. 20-2. Just as we use bandages to cover wounds, we use supportive words and actions to help heal emotional wounds. Psychological first aid involves assisting those who are emotionally distressed, whether due to physical injuries, illness, or overwhelming stress. Signs of emotional distress, like overexcitement, severe fear, excessive worry, deep depression, or anger, can sometimes be less visible than physical injuries but are equally important to address. 20-3. These emotional reactions are indicators that stress is impacting someone's ability to cope effectively. When these symptoms become more pronounced, the need for psychological support becomes more urgent. Knowing how to offer this support is essential, as it can significantly aid in someone's recovery process, just as much as treating a physical ailment. 27BPSYCHOLOGICAL FIRST AID 20-4. You must know how to give psychological first aid to be able to help yourself, your team members, and your unit to keep performing the mission. Psychological first aid measures are simple and easy to understand. Your decision of what to do depends upon your ability to observe the Service member and understand their needs. Making the best use of resources requires ingenuity on your part. A stress reaction resulting in poor judgment can cause injury or even death to yourself or others on the battlefield. It can be even more dangerous if other personnel are affected by the judgment of an emotionally upset Service member. If it is detected early enough, the affected Service member stands a good chance of remaining in their unit as an effective member. If it is not detected early and if the Service member becomes more emotionally upset, they may become a threat to themselves and to others. 172BSITUATIONS REQUIRING PSYCHOLOGICAL FIRST AID 20-5. Psychological first aid (buddy aid) is most needed at the first sign that a Service member cannot perform the mission because of emotional distress. Stress is inevitable in combat, in hostage and terrorist situations, and in civilian disasters such as floods, hurricanes, or industrial accidents. Most emotional reactions to such situations are temporary, and the Service member can still carry on with encouragement. Painful or disruptive symptoms may last for minutes, hours, or days. However, if the stress symptoms are seriously disabling, they may be psychologically contagious and endanger not only the emotionally upset Service member but also the entire unit. 20-6. Sometimes people continue to function well during a disastrous event, but suffer from emotional scars, which impair their job performance or quality of life later. Painful memories and dreams may recur for months and years and still be considered a normal reaction. However, an individual needs treatment if the memories are so painful that the person must avoid all situations which arouse them, becomes socially withdrawn, show symptoms of anxiety, depression, or substance abuse. Experience with police, firefighters, emergency medical technicians, and others who deal with disasters have proved that the routine application of psychological first aid to all the participants, including those who have functioned well, greatly reduces the likelihood of future serious post-traumatic stress disorder(s).

Chapter 20 210 ATP 4-02.11 23 March 2026 173BINTERRELATIONSHIP OF PSYCHOLOGICAL AND PHYSICAL FIRST AID 20-7. Psychological first aid should go together with physical first aid. The discovery of a physical injury or cause for an inability to function does not rule out the possibility of a psychological injury (or vice versa). The person suffering from pain, shock, fear of serious injury, or fear of death does not respond well to joking, indifference, or fearful-tearful attention. Fear and anxiety may take as high a toll of on the Service member's strength as does the loss of blood. 174BGOALS OF PSYCHOLOGICAL FIRST AID 20-8. Psychological First Aid is aimed at supporting Service members in managing immediate stress reactions effectively, ensuring both the well-being of the individual and the operational readiness of the unit. The primary goals of Psychological First Aid are multifaceted, focusing on immediate mental health support, safety, and a swift return to duty. 20-9. The first and foremost goal of Psychological First Aid is to provide empathetic support to Service members experiencing stress reactions. By offering a supportive presence, responders can help individuals navigate their emotional responses effectively. This involves active listening, acknowledging their feelings without judgment, and providing reassurance. This supportive approach is crucial in helping Service members feel understood and less isolated in their experiences. 20-10. Another critical aim of Psychological First Aid is to prevent and control behaviors that could be harmful to the individual or others. This includes identifying signs of distress that might lead to harmful actions and implementing strategies to mitigate these risks. The ability to intervene early and effectively can prevent the escalation of stress reactions into more serious mental health issues, thereby maintaining the safety and cohesion of the unit. 20-11. Finally, Psychological First Aid seeks to return the Service member to duty as efficiently as possible after addressing their immediate psychological needs. This goal underscores the importance of resilience and rapid recovery within military operations, ensuring that personnel are mentally fit to resume their roles. Facilitating a quick return to duty not only helps maintain unit effectiveness but also promotes a sense of normalcy and purpose for the individual, which can be therapeutic in overcoming stress reactions. 175BRESPECT FOR OTHERS’ FEELINGS 20-12. Accept the Service member you are trying to help without censorship or ridicule. Respect their right to their own feelings. Even though your feelings, beliefs, and behavior are different, do not blame or make light of them for the way they feel or act. Your purpose is to help them in this tough situation, not to be their critic. A person does not want to be upset and worried. When they seek help, they need and expect consideration of their fears, not abrupt dismissal, or ridicule. 20-13. Realize that people are the products of a wide variety of factors. All people do not react the same way to the same situations. Everyone has complex needs and motivations, both conscious and unconscious, that are uniquely their own. Often the one thing that finally causes the person to become overloaded by a stressful situation is not the stressor itself, but some other problem. 176BEMOTIONAL AND PHYSICAL DISABILITY 20-14. Accept emotional disability as being just as real as physical disability. If a Service member’s ankle is seriously sprained in a fall, no one expects them to run right away. A Service member’s emotions may be temporarily strained by the overwhelming stress of battle or another traumatic incident. Do not demand that they pull themselves together immediately and carry on without a break. Some individuals can pull themselves together immediately, but others cannot. The Service member whose emotional stability has been disrupted has a disability just as real as the Service member who has sprained their ankle. There is an unfortunate tendency in many people to regard as real only what they can see, such as a wound or bleeding. Some people tend to assume that damage involving a person’s mind and emotions is just imagined, they are not sick or injured, and that they could overcome their trouble by using their will power. 20-15. The phrases “it is all in your head”, “snap out of it”, and “get control of yourself” are often used by people who believe they are being helpful. These terms are expressions of hostility because they show lack

Combat and Operational Stress Control 23 March 2026 ATP 4-02.11 211 of understanding. They only emphasize weakness and inadequacy. The above stated phrases are of no use in psychological first aid. 20-16. Every physically injured person has some emotional reaction to the fact that they are injured. It is normal for an injured person to feel upset. The more severe the injury, the more insecure and fearful they become, especially if the injury is to a body part that is highly valued. For example, an injury to the eyes or the genitals, even though relatively minor, is likely to be extremely upsetting. An injury to some other part of the body may be especially disturbing to an individual for their own reason. For example, an injury to the hand may be a terrifying blow to a surgeon, or an injury to the eye of a pilot. 20-17. An injured Service member can sometimes feel less secure, more anxious, and more afraid not only because of what has happened to them but also what they imagine may happen because of their injury. This fear and insecurity may cause them to be irritable, uncooperative, or unreasonable. As you help the Service member, always keep in mind that such behavior has little or nothing to do with you personally. They need your patience, reassurance, encouragement, and support. 278BCOMBAT AND OPERATIONAL STRESS REACTION 20-18. Stress reaction is a temporary emotional disorder or inability to function, experienced by a previously normal Service member as a reaction to the overwhelming or cumulative stress of combat. Stress reaction gets better with reassurance, rest, physical replenishment, and activities that restore confidence. All Service members are likely to feel stressed under conditions of intense or prolonged stress. They may even become stress reaction casualties and are unable to perform their mission for hours or days. Other combat and operational stress reactions may result in negative behavior, but are not termed stress reaction, as they need treatment that is more intensive. These negative combat and operational stress reactions may result in misconduct and stress behaviors such as drug and alcohol abuse, criminal acts, looting, desertion, and self- inflicted wounds. These harmful combat and operational stress reactions can often be prevented by good psychological first aid. Service members who commit misconduct stress behaviors may require disciplinary action rather than medical treatment. 17BREACTIONS TO STRESS 20-19. Most Service members react to stressful incidents after the situation has passed. Service members feel some fear. This fear may be greater than they have experienced at any other time, or they may be more aware of their fear. In such a situation, they should not be surprised if they feel shaky or become sweaty, nauseated, or confused. These reactions are normal and are not a cause for concern. However, some reactions, either short- or long-term, will cause problems if left unchecked. 403BEmotional Reactions 20-20. The most obvious combat and operational stress reaction is inefficient performance. This can be demonstrated by— • Slow thinking (or reaction time). • Difficulty recognizing priorities and seeing what needs to be done. • Difficulty getting started. • Indecisiveness and having trouble focusing. • Tendency to do familiar tasks and be preoccupied with familiar details. (This can reach the point in which the person is very passive, sitting or wandering, and not knowing what to do). 20-21. A less common reaction may be uncontrolled emotional outbursts; this can be demonstrated by crying, screaming, or laughing. Some Service members will react in the opposite way. They can show signs of being very withdrawn, silent, and try to isolate themselves from everyone. These Service members should be encouraged to remain with their assigned unit. Uncontrolled reactions may appear by themselves or in any combination. The person may be crying uncontrollably one minute and then laughing the next. In this state, the person is restless and cannot keep still. They may run about, apparently without purpose. Inside, they feel a great rage or fear and their physical acts may show this. In their anger, they may indiscriminately strike out at others.

Chapter 20 212 ATP 4-02.11 23 March 2026 404BLoss of Adaptability 20-22. In a desperate attempt to get away from the danger, which has overwhelmed them, a Service member may panic and become confused. Their mental ability may be so impaired they cannot think clearly or even follow simple commands. Their judgment may be faulty, and they may not be aware of their actions, such as standing up in their fighting position during an attack. 20-23. In other cases, overwhelming stress may produce symptoms that are often associated with head injuries. For example, the Service member may appear dazed or be found wandering around aimlessly. They may appear confused and disoriented and may seem to have a complete or partial loss of memory. In such cases, especially when no eyewitnesses can provide evidence that the Service member has NOT suffered a head injury, it is necessary for them to be rapidly evacuated. DO NOT allow the Service members to expose themselves to further personal danger until the cause of the problem has been determined. 405BSleep Disturbance and Repetition of Dreams 20-24. A person who has been overwhelmed by stress, often has difficulty sleeping. The Service member may experience nightmares related to the stressors. Remember that nightmares, in themselves, are not considered abnormal when they occur soon after a period of intensive stress. As time passes, the nightmares usually become less frequent and less intense. In extreme cases, a Service member, even when awake, may think repeatedly of the incident, feel as though it is happening again, and act out parts of their stress repeatedly. 20-25. For some individuals, this repetitious re-experiencing of the stressful event may be necessary for eventual recovery; therefore, it should not be discouraged or viewed as abnormal. For the person re- experiencing the event, such reaction may be disruptive. The Service member needs to be encouraged to ventilate about the incident. Ventilation is a technique where the Service member is given the opportunity to talk extensively and often repetitiously about the experience. 406BSevere Stress or Stress Reaction 20-26. You do not need specialized training to recognize severe stress or stress reaction that will cause problems for the Service member, the unit, or the mission. Reactions that are less severe, however, are more difficult to detect. To determine whether a person needs help, you must observe them to see whether they are doing something meaningful, performing their duties, taking care of themselves, behaving in an unusual fashion, or acting out of character. 178BAPPLICATION OF PSYCHOLOGICAL FIRST AID 20-27. The emotionally disturbed Service member has built a barrier against fear. They do this for their own protection, although they are probably not aware that they are doing it. If they find that they do not have to be afraid and that there are normal, understandable things about them, they will feel safer in dropping this barrier. Persistent efforts to make them realize that you want to understand them will be reassuring, especially if you remain calm. Nothing can cause an emotionally disturbed person to become even more fearful than feeling that others are afraid of them. Try to remain calm. Familiar things, such as a cup of coffee, the use of their name, attention to a minor wound, being given a simple job to do, or the sight of familiar people and activities, will add to their ability to overcome their fear. They may not respond well if you get excited, angry, or abrupt. 407BVentilation 20-28. After the Service member becomes calmer, they are likely to have dreams about the stressful event. They also may think about it when they are awake or even repeat their personal reaction to the event. One benefit of this natural pattern is that it helps them master the stress by going over it just as one master the initial fear of parachuting from an aircraft by doing it repeatedly. Eventually, it is difficult to remember how frightening the event was initially. In giving first aid to the emotionally disturbed Service members, you should let them follow this natural pattern. Encourage them to talk. Be a good listener. Let them tell you, in their own words, what happened. If home front problems or worries have contributed to stress, it will help them to talk about these problems. Your patient listening will prove to the Service member that you are

Combat and Operational Stress Control 23 March 2026 ATP 4-02.11 213 interested in them, and by describing their personal problem, they can work at mastering their fear. If they become overwhelmed, suggest a cup of coffee or a break. Whatever you do, assure them that you will listen again as soon as they are ready. Try to help put the Service member's perception of what happened back into realistic perspective; but DO NOT argue about it. 408BActivity 20-29. A person who is emotionally disturbed as the result of a combat action is a casualty of anxiety and fear. The person may feel as though they are disabled because they have become temporarily overwhelmed by their anxiety. A good way to control fear is through activity. For example, almost all Service members experience a considerable sense of anxiety and fear while they are poised, awaiting the opening of a big offensive; but this is normally relieved, and they feel better once they begin to move into action. They take pride in effective performance and pleasure in knowing that they are a good Service member, perhaps being completely unaware that overcoming their initial fear was their first major accomplishment. 20-30. Useful activity can be very beneficial to Service members who are emotionally disturbed and not physically incapacitated. After you help a Service member get over their initial fear, help them to regain some self-confidence. Help them realize their job continues by finding them something useful to do. Encourage them to be active. Get them to help load trucks, clean up debris, or dig fighting positions. If possible, get them back to their usual duty. Seek out their strong points and help them apply these attributes. Avoid having them just sit around. You may have to provide directions by telling them what to do and where to do it. The instructions should be clear, simple, and should be repeated. A person who has panicked is likely to argue. Respect their feelings, but point out more immediate, obtainable, and demanding needs. Channel their excessive energy and, above all, DO NOT argue. If you cannot get them to become interested in doing profitable work, it may be necessary to enlist aid in controlling their over-activity before it results in more panic. Prevent the spread of such infectious feelings by restraining and segregating if necessary. 20-31. Involvement in an activity helps the Service member in three ways; they— • Place their thoughts on something more productive. • Have an outlet for their excessive tensions. • Prove to them that they can do something useful. 409BRest 20-32. There are times, particularly in combat, when physical exhaustion is a principal cause for emotional reactions. A unit sleep plan should be established and implemented. When possible, Service members should be given a safe and relatively comfortable area in which to sleep. Examples would be an area away from heavy traffic, noise, congestion, a place that is clean, dry, and protected from environmental conditions. The more uninterrupted sleep a Service member gets the better they will be able to function in the tactical environment. 410BHygiene 20-33. Field hygiene is an important ingredient in a Service member's morale. A Service member who is lacking personal hygiene will not function as well as others who have had the opportunity to bathe and put on clean, dry clothing. During combat, unit leaders should stress the importance of personal hygiene. Good personal hygiene not only improves morale, but it is also a preventive measure against disease and disease and nonbattle injury. 41BGroup Activity 20-34. You have probably already noticed that a person who works, faces danger, and handles serious problems better if they are a member of a closely-knit group. Each Service member in the team supports the other team members. Esprit de corps is built because the Service members have the same interests, goals, and mission. As a result, they are more productive; and are less worried because everyone is involved. This is one of the most effective tools you have in your psychological first aid bag. Getting the Service member back into the team or squad activities will re-establish their sense of belonging and security. This will go far toward making them a useful member of the unit.

Chapter 20 214 ATP 4-02.11 23 March 2026 179BREACTIONS AND LIMITATIONS 20-35. Up to this point, the discussion has been primarily about the feelings of the emotionally distressed Service member. What about your feelings towards them? Whatever the situation, you will have emotional reactions (conscious or unconscious) toward this Service member. Your reactions can either help or hinder your ability to help them. When you are tired or worried, you may very easily become impatient with them if they are unusually slow or exaggerated. You may even feel resentful toward them. Physical wounds can be seen and easily accepted. Emotional reactions are more difficult to accept as injuries. On the other hand, you tend to be overly sympathetic. Excessive sympathy for an incapacitated person can be as harmful as negative feelings in your relationship with them. They need strong help, but not your sorrow. To overwhelm them with pity may make them feel even more inadequate. You must expect your buddy to recover, to be able to return to duty, and to become a useful Service member again. This expectation should be displayed in your behavior and attitude as well as in what you say. If they can see your calmness, confidence, and competence, they will be reassured and will feel a sense of greater security. For more information on stress reactions see tables 20-1, table 20-2 on page 215 and table 20-3 on page 216. Table 20-1. Mild Stress Reaction PHYSICAL SIGNS* EMOTIONAL SIGNS* 1. Trembling, tearful. 1. Anxiety, indecisiveness. 2. Jumpiness, nervousness. 2. Irritable, complaining. 3. Cold sweat, dry mouth. 3. Forgetful, unable to concentrate. 4. Pounding heart, dizziness. 4. Easily startled by noise, movement. 5. Insomnia, nightmares. 5. Grief, tearful. 6. Nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. 6. Anger, beginning to lose confidence in self and unit. 7. Fatigue. 8. Thousand-yard stare. 9. Difficulty thinking, speaking, and communicating. SELF- AND BUDDY AID 1. Continue mission performance and focus on the immediate mission. 2. Expect Service members to perform the assigned duties. 3. Always remain calm; be directive, and in control. 4. Rapid and/or inappropriate talking. 2. Flinching or ducking at sudden sounds. 2. Argumentative, reckless movements, or actions. 3. Shaking, trembling (whole body or arms). 3. Inattentive to personal hygiene. 4. Cannot use parts of the body, no physical reason (hands, arms, or legs). 4. Indifferent to danger. 5.
