If a Service member’s behavior endangers the mission, self, or others, do whatever is necessary to control them. 2. If the Service member is upset, calmly talk them into cooperating. 3. If concerned about the Service member’s reliability: • Unload their weapon. • Take weapons if seriously concerned. • Physically restrain them only when necessary for safety or transportation. 4. Chapter 20 216 ATP 4-02.11 23 March 2026 Table 20-3. Preventive Measures to Combat and Operational Stress Reaction Preventive Measures 1. Welcome new Service members into your team and get to know them quickly. If you are new, be active in making friends. 2. Be physically fit (strength, endurance, and agility). 3. Know and practice lifesaving self- and buddy aid. 4. Practice rapid relaxation techniques. 5. Help each other out when things are tough at home or in the unit. 6. Keep informed; ask your leader questions, ignore rumors. 7. Work together to give everyone food, water, shelter, hygiene, and sanitation. 8. Sleep when the mission and safety permit; let everyone get time to sleep. Follow these sleep rules: • Sleep only in safe places and by standard operating procedure. • If possible, sleep six to nine hours per day. • Try to get at least four hours of sleep per day. • Get good sleep before going on sustained operations. • Take a nap when you can but allow time to wake up fully. • Catch up on sleep after going without. 180BSUPPORTING AT-RISK SERVICE MEMBERS 20-36. Taking care of fellow Service members is a fundamental duty within the DOD, emphasizing the critical role of teamwork and the inherent value of each individual. Essential to this dynamic is the implementation of the battle-buddy concept, particularly when addressing COSR. Vigilance, appropriate intervention, and thorough follow-through are key elements in fostering a supportive environment. 20-37. The optimal initial response to Service member stress involves the caring and observant presence of battle buddies and leaders. The DOD supports this approach through a robust framework that extends from individual Service members to the highest levels of leadership, facilitating COSC. It is imperative that Service members recognize signs of distress among their peers, seek help, and provide consistent support. 20-38. In the context of handling COSRs, the "ACE" acronym—standing for Acknowledge, Care, and Escort—serves as a concise and memorable strategy. This method is crucial for both Service members and leaders in managing stress reactions effectively: • Acknowledge: The first critical step is recognizing potential stress reactions in colleagues. This requires alertness to behavioral and emotional shifts that may suggest a Service member is struggling. Trusting one’s instincts and taking any signs of distress seriously are essential in this initial phase. • Care: After recognizing a colleague's distress, providing immediate support is vital. This support can include offering reassurance, listening with empathy, and creating a safe, non-judgmental environment for the individual to share their experiences. It’s important to affirm that their reactions are normal responses to the stressful situations they have encountered. • Escort: The final step involves guiding the affected Service member to suitable professional resources. This could mean directing them to a mental health expert, a chaplain, or another unit leader who can offer further support and advice. Ensuring the individual receives appropriate help is crucial and helps to mitigate any stigma associated with seeking mental health support. 20-39. The Acknowledge, Care, and Escort framework underscores the importance of timely intervention and the need to connect distressed Service members with suitable resources. It offers a practical guide for those who may lack extensive mental health training but are committed to assisting their colleagues. 20-40. The Acknowledge, Care, and Escort approach is a preliminary measure and does not substitute for professional mental health evaluation and treatment. Involving mental health professionals is crucial for a comprehensive assessment and care of Service members experiencing COSRs, ensuring they receive the full spectrum of necessary support.

Appendix B 21BRescue Equipment 282BWARRIOR AID AND LITTER KIT B-1. The warrior aid and litter kit (WALK) (figure B-1) allows first aid treatment and immediate evacuation of one patient in a CASEVAC vehicle and treatment of multiple trauma patients at the POI. The total weight of the WALK can weigh approximately 29 pounds, 15 ounces. The WALK offers an option for a vehicle life-saving kit. Figure B-1. Warrior aid and litter kit B-2. The system holds a quad-fold litter (see figure B-2 on page 225) and a pocket system containing medical supplies. The WALK contains a hypothermia prevention kit to help stabilize patients during transport. The WALK also includes the following: • Five pairs of nitrile trauma gloves. • Two NPAs, size 28 French with lubricant. • One casualty equipment bag. • Two CoTCCC approved occlusive chest seals. • Two combat application TQs. • Six trauma dressings, six inches. • Four rolls of rolled gauze, 4.5 inches by 4.1 yards. 23 March 2026 ATP 4-02.11 221

Figure B-2. Quad-fold litter B-3. The WALK fits into any standard or nonstandard CASEVAC asset and is useful as part of the prepositioning of medical supplies or cache on a forward operating base, CCP, or at a patrol base. 283BPOLYMER FLEXIBLE LITTER SYSTEM B-4. The CoTCCC approved polymer flexible litter system (figure B-3 on page 226) uses a sled design to allow the evacuator to continue returning fire as the casualty is evacuated. It is used for confined space, high angle, or technical rescue, and it provides casualty protection while allowing the aid and litter teams to have their hands free for weapons and security. 225 ATP 4-02.11 23 March 2026

(ATP 4-02.4). *care under fire The first phase of care in tactical combat casualty care where very limited care is provided for the casualty while the enemy threat is still active. Also known as CUF or care under threat. casualty Any person who is lost to the organization by having been declared dead, duty status – whereabouts unknown, excused absence-whereabouts unknown, missing, ill, or injured. (JP 4-02). casualty collection point A location that may or may not be staffed, where casualties are assembled for evacuation to a medical treatment facility. (ATP 4-02.2). casualty evacuation (Joint) The unregulated movement of casualties aboard any vehicle. Also called CASEVAC. (JP 4-02). (Army) The movement of casualties aboard nonmedical vehicles or aircraft without en route medical care. (ATP 4-02.13). *casualty response The immediate and organized care, evacuation and reporting of those injured or killed in action. *combat lifesaver (Joint) Nonmedical Department of Defense person who has received additional trauma training and equipment, providing enhanced medical treatment beyond self-aid/buddy aid. (JP 4-02). (Army) A Soldier trained and equipped to provide enhanced first aid as a secondary mission, known as CLS. *first aid The immediate lifesaving measures performed on casualties or military working animals. first responder Is anyone who provides initial and immediate treatment to self or others. (JP 4-02). medical evacuation The timely and effective movement of the wounded, injured, or ill to and between medical treatment facilities on dedicated and properly marked medical platforms with en route care provided by medical personnel. Also called MEDEVAC. (ATP 4-02.2). medical treatment facility (Joint) A facility established for the purpose of furnishing medical and/or dental care to eligible individuals. Also called MTF. (JP 4-02). (Army) Any facility established for the purpose of providing medical treatment. (FM 4-02). patient (Joint) A sick, injured, wounded, or other person receiving medical care, dental care, or other medical treatment. (JP 4-02). (Army) A patient is a wounded, ill and injured Soldier who receives medical care or treatment from medically trained personnel. (ATP 4-02.10). 23 March 2026 ATP 4-02.11 229

Glossary 230 ATP 4-02.11 23 March 2026 tactical combat casualty care The deliberate integration of tactics and medicine to treat casualties during combat. Also called TCCC. (JP 4-02). *tactical evacuation care The third phase of care in tactical combat casualty care. Care provided during transportation from the battelefield to a medical treatment facility. *tactical field care The second phase of care in tactical combat casualty care. Care provided once the threat has been neutralized, the scene is safe or the casualty has moved or been moved out of the immediate threat situation. Also known as TFC. triage Triage is the system of sorting and prioritizing casualties based on the tactical situation, mission, and available resources (FM 4-02).
